CLOUDS IN PROSPECT. BY TRU LATE FRANCES RIDLEY HAVERGAL. Oh, pleasant have the hours of my early childhood been, When all around me seemed enrobed in brightly glittering sheen; 'When a thousand rainbow tints were in every simple flower, And a thousand new delights came with every sunny hour; When I thought the merry birds trided their carols all for me, .id with heart and voice I joined in their joyous melody; When, all heedless of the darkening storm, I loved the purple cloud, And listened with delight to the thunder pealing loud. In those happy days of childhood, I did not think or see That many trials might be waiting even then for me; But now, though yet I meet them not, I know that they mot stand In many v. varied shape and form, unseen, on ev'ry hand. As yet from heavy troubles, thank God, I have been free; Oh, surely there are few who have what is vouchsafed to me! But one eclipse hatla shadowed o'er my childhood's Bunny hours, And now its sharpness seemeth past, that thdria 'mid many flowers. But still the saddening feeling cometh oftener than before, That many a future sorrow e'en for me may be in store. For all around me seem to have some wearing care or grief, From which they scarcely dare to hope on earth to find
_ relief, _ And my memory loves to dwell upon the merry, careless hours When l_thonght the world a thornie,3B garden of lovely
flown-ie. . —Sunday Magazine.

The rogue was not a little dieconceited at heating a loea laugh from the occupant of the apartment, whom he supposed fast asleep. Why do you laugh?" asked the thief.—" I ant remelting, met good fellow," said Balzec, " to think what pains you are taking, and what risk you run, in hope of findraginoney by night in a desk where the lawful owner cannot find any by day." The thief at once left. A tutor of one of the Oxford colleges, who limped in his walk, was some years ago accosted by a well-known politi- cian, who mired him if he was not the chaplain of the col- lege at Belch a time, naming the yeer. The doctor replied that he was. The interrogator observed, "I knew you by your limp." "Well," said the doctor, "It seems my limp- ing,made a deeper impression than my preaching." " Ah, doctor,", was the reply, with ready wit, "it is the highest compliment we can pay a minister, to say that he is known by his walk rather than by his conversation." There are a few simple-minded ones among the Dutch Boers of South Africa. One of them, a short time back, suffered himself to be convinced that a ready-reckoner holds good only for a single year, like an almanac. Having to adjust accounts with a Jew woolstapler, the latter made a mistake in accounts very much to his own advantage. The Boor therefore produced a reedy-reckoner and pointed out the blunder, But the Israelite was not to be beaten. "Oh, that's a ready-reckoner of last year's date," was the reply; *We all wrong for this year." And the Burr, believing the ataternent, gave up the point, and was duly victimised. THE LAST DAY OF THE YEAR ONE THOUSAND.—The labourers in the field and the artisans in the towns could not be induced te go about their work with any regularity (netwithstandina, that their daily bread depended upon it), I lorlinkieg of the outbreak of Divine wrath which was abo to-take place. The terrified and conscience striken mai rid no heed to remonstrances, but gathered eagerly rotted fanetic moaks or half-crazed pilgrims, who poured into their ears their tale of horrors, ever growing more wild andeterribler as the last week of the year 1,000 went by. Whine the last day of that week dawntsd, the madness had attained its height, All work, of whatsoever kind, was SUS. pendeon The market places were deserted; the shops were sihnt ; the tables were not spread for 'nests; the very house- hold fires remained unlighted. Men when they met in the streets searcely saw or spoke to one another. Their eyes had, a wild stare in them as though they expected every moment some terrible manifestation to take place. A strange unnatural silence prevailed everywhere except in the churchea, which were already thronged with eager devotees, , who prostrated themselves before the shrines of their /e,vourite minter imploring their protection daring the fear- Ica scenes which were on the point of being displayed. As the day wore on the number of those who alright admission grew greater and greater, until every corner of the sacred edifices, large as these were, was densely crowded, and it became impossible to find room for more. But the multitude outside still stove and clamoured for ad- mission, filling the ;porches and doorways, and climb- ing up the buttresses to find a refuge on the roofs which they could not obtain inside. It WM gene- rally believed that the expected loosing 0 Satan would take place at some time or other before the night was endedebat at what precise moment no one could stay. A strange and solemn commentary on the text which bids men to watch, because "they know not whether the Maeter cd the house will come at even, or at midnight, 02 at cockcrowing, or in the morning," was presented by the mul- titudes which filled the churches that night. Watch in very truth they did. Not an eye was closed throughout that lengthened vigil; not a knee but EMS bent in humblest sappticatton ; not a voice but joined the penitential chant, or put up a fervent entreaty for help and protection. There were no clocks in those days; bat the flight of the hours was marked by great waxen taper" with metal balls attached at intervals to them. These fell, one after another, as the flames reached the strings by which they were secured, into • brazen basin beneath, with a clang which resounded Wench the elleee At the recurrence of each of these eremengeponneee'ehe awe of the vast apembly seemed to eceepen and intensify aa_each realised the terrible fact that between. hien *Ad the Outtenret of Divine wrath only the briefest interval Cllald now remain. At last the night, long as it was, began to draw to an end. The chill which pre- cedes daybreak pervaded the air, and in the eastern sky the first pale gleans of morning began to show itself. This must be ple eignal for the long pent-up anger of Heaven to show itself, Satan was even now being loosed from his bondage, But no; the light grew stronger in the heavens, and the flame of the candles paled before it, and at last the rays of the risen son streamed through the windows and fell on the White, anxious fates of the watchers. The night had passed away. A new day, a new year,a new century had began.— at Home. Briefly, Mr. Jones's process I consists in the painless injection, by meansof a flexible tube, of boracic acid into the jugular vein of an animal prior to its slaughter. The preservative fluid being thus made to flow into the animal's system while it is alive, the action of the heart conveys the antiseptic through the blood vessels to every portion of the frame. Many advantages, it is said, result from the application of this process, not the least being, in the opinion of scientific authorities who have wit- nessed the operation, that the animal suffers less than by any present mode of killing. The appearance of the carcase when "dressed" is in all respects similar to that of meat as ordinarily prepared by butchers for market. The flesh of the carcase retaine its firm,' natural qualities at ordinary temperature from one month to six weeks in summer, and from two or three months in cold weather. Treated by Mr. Jones's process, meat becomes very tender from keeping, and the good flavour and juiciness are remarkable. It has, as alleged, further been found, through carefully-made experi- ments, that meat thus preserved or cured keeps, even after being cooked, sweet and palatable a much longer time than fieeh killed in the ordinary way. A number of scientific and professional men have testified to the value of Mr. Jones's process, and to the excellence of the meat preserved by it. Among these may be mentioned Professor Hunting, Dr. Francis T. Bond, M.D., and Mr. J. T. Bridgman, M.R.C.S.L. Professor Wanklyn has certified that "the meat preserved by the process is perfectly cafe and whole- Some," while the harmlessness of boracic acid is further proved by the experiments of Professor Barff, who partook daily of milk and cream preserved by it and found no ill , effects result therefrom. , THEI ENGLISH CART HORSE SOCIETY'S 8l".1-OW, 1884.—The official report of the English gall EiiirtW ',Society's recent show shows that the entries for tfils,'Vrar'e ehow gave an increase of 118 stallions over last iatae. apd the cost, which has been diminishing, will not exceed £275. The importance to trade and commerce of the well-being of agriculture has received the strongest possible proof during the last few • years, the principal hindrance to the prosperity Of all kinds of manufactures having been the scarcity of money or money's worth of produce from the land, as for the last few years several millions of pounds have been lost to the country in paying for that which in ordinary seasons would have been produced at home, without the slightest increase in the outlay, and, in fact, in many instances with a de- creased expenditure of farmers' capital. CHOOSING HUSBANDS AND WrvEs.—Of one thing girls may be sure, and that is that the young men who make the best sons and brothers will also make the best husbands. And young men may be equally sure that those girls who are the best daughters and sisters will also, as a rule, be the best wives. If a young man, before he is married, is desti- tute of those affections and principles which come out in filial obedience, courtesy, and a controlling sense of duty, he will be equally destitute of them after he is married. The mere fact of wedlock will not change the fundamental prin. ciples of his nature. He will be essentially the same human being after marriage—or, at least, after the honeymoon— that he was before it. The same principles hold true with regard to women. She who is selfish and vain and idle and deceitful as a girl, will be pretty apt to be the curse of the man who marries her; while the girl who is dutiful to her parents, and industrious and unselfish and truthful, will be almost certain to be a blessing to him who gets her for a wife.

THE LOGIC OF PAlN.—Pain is the protector of the voicelesa tissues! It tells us to desist from efforts when they are becoming injurious; it teaches us to avoid what is destructive to the tissues; it compels us to rest injured parts, and so to permit of their repair. Pain, then, is very far from an unmitigated evil. Without the sensitive skin ' in which our bodies are enclosed, injury would constantly be inflicted upon the tissues; and without the lessons taught us by pain, there is every reason to believe thst most mis- chievous and injurious acts would be constantly committed. Take neuralgia for instance. It may be the outcome of several conditions which have to be discriminated for its relief. In the young and in early adult life it is almost always the result of imperfect tissue•natrition, however caused. Romberg wrote with equal poetical feeling and scientific truth, "Pain is the prayer of a nerve for healthy I blood," and neuralgia is the common outcome of blood either poverty-stricken or poisoned by some deleterious in- gredients, as in material poisoning for instance. Without the pain so produced the condition would go on unrelieved, and ulterior organic chinges would probably be brought about. But pain impels the sufferer to seek relief.—Dr. Fotheryill in " Contemporary Review" for May. KEEPING A Cow.—l can remember (said Henry Ward Beecher) when I received an old cow in payment of a bad debt. It was a very bad debt, and I came to consider it a bad payment. She was a thin cow, but the former owner said she was better than she looked, being a cross between a I Jersey and a Durham. She In oked as if she might have been a cross between an old hair trunk and an abandoned hoop. skirt. I kept the brute three days, and no one except perhaps Lieutenant Atwell, could ever appreciate the suffer- ing I endured in that time. The first night she broke through the fence, ar.d reduced to a pulp all the under- clothing belonging to my next door neighbour. She pat her horns through my bath tub, and ate up all my geraniums. She was to give three gallons of milk a day, but she seemed to be short just then, and never had that to spire while we kept her. The second day she walked into the kitchen, upset pan of butter and a tub of lard. Then she fell down a well, and when I got her out, at the cost of five dollars, she took the colic, whooping cough, or some- thing, and kept us awake all night. Not a greetothing was left in my garden; my neighbour's peach trees and the rope on which his underware grew were as bare of fruit as a single-tree, and he did not have a twig of shrubbery left. My neighbour came over to see me, and said, "Now, I don't desire any quarrel, but I Want you to keep your cow out of my shrubbery." a And I Want you, my friend," said I," to keep your shrubbery out of my cow; it spoils the taste of the milk." Ever afterwards there wise a coolness between us, and any neighbour's wife ceased to patronise our house when she wanted to borrow a cupful of yeast powder. The medical profession are now ordering Cadbury's Cocos Essence in thousands of camel, because it contains more nutri- s oue and fiesh-f rming elernenie than any other beverage, and is preferable to the thick starchy cisme ordinarily sold. When you ask for Cadbury's Cocoa Essence be sure that yOu get it, as shopkeepers often push Imitations for the sake of extra pref'ts. Makers to the Queen. Paris Depot, 90, Faubourg et. II onore.—Aart. •

;R, SATURDAY, NIA w- s COTTAGEITARDFNING inns' SHOW of Fruit and Vegetables, on a large 'iv-. be held at the Royal Horticultural Society's Gardens, South Kensington, London, on the 12th of August next. There are 36 classes, and one which should be a show of itself is open to the various cottage garden societies in the country, or any horticultural society with which that class of exhibitors may be allied. There are six prizes in this special class, the premier one being £5. The officers of any society may collect the produce of its members and for- ward it to the secretary of the society, or, better still, one of them or more may accompany the exhibits and see that they are properly staged. The prizes, we presume, will be handed over to the parties representing the successful coin. petitors, and it is left to the contributing members how they shall be distributed. The date of the show is favourable to northern growers so far as vegetables are concerned. SCARLET RUNNER BEANS may with safety be sown now. On light gravelly soil special preparation should be made for them by making trenches similar to those used for , Celery, only they should be deeper and filled up to the ear- face with layers of manure and soil alternately, and in the centre of this trench the Beans are planted four inches deep. It is also a good plan before commencing to dig the last row Of Celery to place a good layer of manure on each side, so that as the trench is levelled the manure is covered. The soil placed on the top being also good, an excellent bed is formed for either Scarlet Runners or Peas. There is an ob- jection to making a row of the Beans in small gardens on account of the height they grow, and the expense of sticks to support them, which we admit is costly. We consider nets cheaper than sticks. Fences may also be utilised to , give them support, and the row, instead of running north ' and south, and obstructing the rays of the sun, may be placed at the northern boundary of the garden, with its ends east and west. Another good arrangement is to have sun- dry circular clumps, the sticks being usually placed first round a circle two feet diameter in a sloping manner, so I that they meet at the top and be tied together, which in- creases their power to resist strong winds. THE Faosm GARDEN.—The sooner Calceolarias and Ver- benas are planted out the better. If the former do not get established before the warm weather sets in they are apt to succumb. Verbenas will commence to root at once, and consequently will begin to flower all the sooner, and will continue to do so until the first sharp frost checks them. We risked some plants of each out more than a fortnight ago, and we find them progressing. Polyanthus and Hardy Primroses may be sown now. Some prefer this season of the year to the autumn. We have been successful both ways, and when the packet of seed will admit we would sow 1 some now and some later on. The advantages urged in favour of sowing now are that a much stronger plant is secured and that they flower earlier, and for the latter rea- son we advocate an autumn or later sowing to supply suc- cessional bloom. We prefer to sow in boxes, and in the ab- sence of a glass frame we would cover the box over with sheets of glass. The seed only require a light covering of soil, but they must be kept moist, and to obviate frequent waterings the glass should be covered over with any fabric I that will exclude light. It will be as well to explain that we do not mean the common Wild Primrose, but the new race of hardy ones which are becoming so fashionable. Some very good samples of them were exhibited at the Preston Spring Flower Show, by Mr. Gooch, of Bamber Bridge. Wallflowers sown now and in a month hence, out of doors in each case, will flower next spring and form a succession. Some of the earliest sown will frequently throw up odd spikes late in the autumn and during mild winters. Some Double German sown this time last year are now in full flower and are of various shades, diffusing their frag- rance all around them. Though perhaps not so powerful as the old Single English Variety, we prefer these for general purposes. THE WlNDOW.—Balsams may be successfully raised and cultivated in the window, and the task will be easier if the seeds are placed two or three in a two or three-inch pot, using as many pots as the number of plants required. When the plants are well up, select the best and the one nearest the centre of the pot for the future specimen, and pall the others up. We are aware the usual practice is to sow dozens of seed in a pot, and when two or three inches high turn them out and separate them, and pot singly in small pots. Owing to their necessarily crowded state in the seed pot, many of the plants, especially those near the centre, are spoiled, which is obviated by adopting the method we ad- vise. Moreover, in the operation of separating, the young roots being so matted together are unavoidably so damaged that the plants hang down their heads, and for days refuse to be reconciled to their fresh quarters, whilst our plants that were thinned in the pots will be making rapid progress, and will not require moving till the pots are harts, tilled with roots. Balsam seed require a Dot rich sandy soil to grow in, which may increase in stiffness and richness every time the plants are transferred to larger pots.

GEESE. The goose is such a favourite article of diet, that any- thing which deals with it is sure to be of interest. We give the following extract from a French poultry journal, which in the form of questions and answers will inculcate many lessons which will be of service to our readers : "Is it possible to have a flock of geese (say from 100 to 150) at liberty on a large estate, returning home every evening, and intended as egg producers; or whether it is , indispensable to isolate men productive family, as it is said , the males fight furiously. In any case, how many females I are to be associated with the male ?" Geese in flocks live in perfect harmony during the rearing period, but such agglomeration would be profitless at the breeding season; worse than that, for it would eipose one to a thorough disappointment. To insure success, the goose requires quiet, and to be made comfortable. Tne ganders that live in good intelligence during the whole of the summer and autumn become very quarrelsome at the first cold weather, and are always fighting most viciously during the laying season. The result of this fighting is the non•fecundity of the eggs. We maintain that with a 11 lck of 100 geese and 20 ganders, the produc- tion would be far inferior to that of two or three little lots separated and kept in a proper manner. A running stream appears to us indispensable during the laying season, with. oat which the majority of the eggs would be clear. On a sheet of water a gander can serve five geese, otherwise he could only have three at most. A goose of a good breed may lay thirty to thirty-five eggs, most of which would be fertile, if kept in a healthy condition—that is, if she has a good grass run, good corn, and good water. Construct four runs, separated from each other, with five geese and a gander in each. You will then be able to rely on a sufficient number of goslings to make a fine flock for the following season. Mind you do not work your young ganders; they must be two years old, otherwise almost all the eggs would be clear. - -

"Is it possible to distinguish by any outward signs the gander from the goose, when young ?" In the common breeds, not crossed with the Toulouse, the male is always white, and is known as soon as his feathers begin to grow, but the female is not completely white. In the Toulouse breed., the male and female are exactly alike; it is only by their gait they are recognised, and even then it is when they are almost adults. "In the artificial incubation of the eggs of geese, are not there certain special points to be noticed, such as an average heat leas than that usually employed for hens' eggs, or any special care at the time of hatching ?" The arti- ficial hatching of the eggs of geese is easy and regular. One condition is necessary—viz., the eggs must be very fresh, and must not have travelled. The hatching takes place without the least difficulty or special care. Notwith- standing this, our advice is not to hatch the eggs of geese by artificial incubation; there will exist no advantage whatever. You cannot forward the hatching as with hens' eggs; the goose lays only at her season; she sits naturally, and generally well, and rears her young with a care and solicitude quite remarkable. . The gosling requires to roam in the fields from its birth. Under these circumstances the artificial mother would be less useful than its natural mother. In incubating artificially, one is prone to believe that an early second laving is anticipated; not so—whether the goose is free or brings up a troop of goslings, the time of her second laying will not vary. Artificial incubation is a useful accessory, we may even say indispensable, fora surplus of eggs, Or at the time of hatching when certain over-anxious mothers stifle the young ones at their birth, but as far as the eggs of geese are concerned, we consider artificial incubation quite useless. Upon the whole, the rearing of geese, with all the advantages of land and water, extent of common, and in proximity of cornfields at harvest time, is one of the most profitable that can be undertaken. In yards where sitting varieties of fowls are kept it will be an advantage to no allow the hens to hatch out a lot of chickens This is not for the sake of the chickens them- ' selves, for those hatched out in the latter part of June eel- dons do well, the heat apparently being too much for them, , but in order to give the hens a rest Of course, if a hen has brought tip one or two hatches during the spring it will not be necessary to do this, but if she has been laying all the time the rest from laying for eight or ten weeks will strengthen the system and hasten on the moult, thus ad- vancing the time when the hens will commence laying in , the autumn. To force the hens to continue laying without cessation does not pay in the long run. The chickens when hatched can be killed or reared, and will come in for Christ- man or earlier.

THE STORY OF BIANCA CAPELLO.-With the Pitt Palace is linked the romantically tragic story of Bianco Capello, the beautiful Venetian lady wh r, at the early age of 16, ran away from home and friends in company with a banker's clerk. Varied fortunes succeeded, till she even- tually became Grand Duchess of Tuscany. Only one thing was now longed for to complete her happiness, and that was the birth of an heir to the Grand Decal throne. Bat this event was long waited for ig vain, and at length the father- confessor of the lady was prevailed upon to bring to the palace a new-born infant in his capacious sleeve. Bat Car- dinal Ferdinand, who was next in succession, had his sus- picions. He met the monk on his arrival, and gave him a close embrace, which discovered the plot. At a subsequent banquet, Bianca set before the cardinal a dish of pastry which she had prepared with her own hand. It is said that the cardinal's.opal ring betrayed to him the lurking danger, and he politely declined. Whereupon :the Grand Dike de- clared that it should not be said that the Duchess had made her pastry for nothing, and Amgen eating it himself. The lady could not stop him, with that wary cardinal's eye fixed on her. She resolved to share her husband's fate, par- took with him of the poisoned dish, and in the morning they were both dead.—Cities of the World.

In common with the rest of the world, Dr. M—, an eminent Church of Bcotland divine, visited the Paris E. hibition. Shortly after his arrival in the gay metropolis, an Irishman came running up to him in the street, crying, " Och, blessings on ye, Dochtor —! How are yea !" "I'm very well," repliAd the doctor, rather drily. "And when did yea come to Paris ?" "Last week. Bat how do you come to know me?" "Give me a shilling, and I'll tell vfa." THE AUSTRALIAN CRICKETER.I.—At Sheffield Park, near Uckfield, on Tuesday, the Australians won the first match of their present tour in England, defeating the strong English eleven selected by Lord Sheffield, by an innings and siz runs to spare. LIBERALISM AT YORE.—Mr. Lockwood, Q.C., on Monday night addressed a meeting of some 4,000 Liberal electors of York, in the great hall of the Exhibi lien Building, cn politi- cal questions. He was most enthusiastically received, and was almost unanimously accepted as one of the Liberal can- didates for the city at the next election. ENGLAND AND THE SOUDAN.---The International Arbitra- tion Association, at a meeting at Manchester, have adopted a resolution expressing satisfaction at the sroa attitude taken by Her Majesty's Government in refusing to send British troops to perish in the Soudan, and hoping that they will withstand the clamours of those who are ever ready t° make pretexts for war. _ _

_ A SURGEON SENT TO GAOL.—At Leeds Assizes, on Satur- day, Robert Locke Evans, a Sheffield surgeon, was convicted of manslaughter in respect of the death of a woman who had died in her confinement. The prisoner was alleged to have been guilty of gross neglect, which was attributed to bis having been the worse for drink while in attendance upon the deceased. He had been incarcerated a month, and was committed for five months larger. SAVAGERY AT SEA —At Leeds Assizes, on MendaY; Joseph Nicholin and Thomas Hardisty, skieper and " thif" hand" respectively of a Hull fishing smack, were indicted for murdering a youth named Rowbottom, engaged on board the smock as cook. It was stated that after going to sea the prisoners barbarously ill-treated the lad, kicking hi° about the deck, jumping upon him with their heavy Ben- boots, and depriving him of proper food. On February lath Rowbottom was found dead in the hold, and Nicholin Con- cocted a story about his having fallen upon a barrel and $o received fatal injuries. The body was examined when taken to Hull, and in addition to bruises in every part there wetss found fractures of the ribs and other internal injuries erbica were evidently the result of distinct ast wits, and had been the cause of death. The trial had not concluded when the , court adjourned, but was terminated on Tuesday. The,. jury, after a lengthened absence, reduced the crime to one of manslaughter ; and Mr. Justice Hawkins, in sentencing! the prisoners to penal servitude for life, said they had been r guilty of as brutal and diabolical a crime as it was possible for the mind to cenceive. A Cuarous Cusroist—lt is well known that in the olden times many holiday diversions, and even occasionally fairs' For • were held within the precincts of our parish churches. Instance, in the registers at Winchester there is to be seen 3 copy of a mandate from William of Wykeham, which for- bids juggling, the performance of loose den !es, ballad mg; ing, the exhibiting of profane shows and spectacles, snd celebration of other games, in the church and even in the churchyard of Kingston-on-Thames, on pain of excommuni- cation. It would appear, however, that even this strong measure did not prevent the origin, or at all events the , practice, of another ancient custom, of which little or no• thing is known except that it is thought to have been pectr liar to Kingston, but which w 45 carried on iii the church Itself, even during the time of divine service, down to the end of the last century, if not to the beginning of this. The congregation, strange as it may sound, used to crack nuts during service on the Sunday next before the eve of St. Michael's Day. Hence that Sunday was called " Crack-nut Sunday." The custom was not restrain,4 or confined to the • younger branches of the congregation, but was practised " alike by young and old; and it is on record that the noiee I caused by the cracking was often so loud and so powerful as • to oblige the minister to break off for a time his reading or his sermon until silence was restored. The above custoln was thought by one or two a-ntiquaries to have been con- nected in some way or other with the choosing of bailiffs and other members of the dorporate body on Michaelmas . Day, and with the usual feast which attended that proceed' ing.—CasseWs greater London. THE PUBLIC LIBRARY.—HOW TO USE IT.—StIpPOSe yourself in the presence of an army of fifty thousand men. Suppose that army on dress parade—each company, regl" ment, and battalion arranged in perfect order; each resem- bling the others in file and rank and in its individual men. Suppose you have come down many miles from home to see a brother who is one of these soldiers; how will you find I him among these fifty thousand? The wrong way will be the one you will most naturally take; so we will watch you as you go down the long line of faces, looking eager' into each for a sign of recognition. You pass from regi- ment to regiment, sod a half-day passes while you are log for one man in fifty thousand. After several hours of useless search, you begin to wonder if it would not be a good idea to find some one who knew something about the lona' tion of the army, and could direct you to the proper place. A staff-officer comes dashing by at this moment, and inti hail him with an inquiry; but he has business of another nature, and only says. "Go to head-quarters." This 9.011 do, and to the officer on duty you repeat your inquiry. l'05; sibly he may know your brother personally, and can On'. to his exact location. More probable that he does not kfic# him; in which case he calls up the Adjutant, and places the matter in his hands. He looks over some rolls and list* upon which he finds your brother's name enrolled in Coil' pany —, Leeds Volunteers. Cross, from Baptist congregations, Bolton. THE CHANNEL TUNNEL SCHEME.

... -. Sir E. Wkrzrx, in moving the second reading of the South-Eastern and Charnel Tunnel Railway Bill, said the measure, though nominally a private one, was really a great national scheme,, involving one of those questions which justified the House in aslimg the Government for a declara- tion of policy. He pointed out that galleries 2,000 yards in length had already been projected under the bed of the Channel, both from the French and the English side, and I warned the Government against rejecting this bill, and leav- ing it to France, if she chose, to go on with her part of excavation. The bed of the channel, according to the highest authorities on intainational law, belonged to the first finder; therefore, if the French Governmeet projected a tunnel up to the shores of kingland, it wotod be an exten- elan of the French Empire, and the tunnel would be go- verned by French law. As An additional inducement to the Government to look favourably on the scheme, be submitted that in the opinion of geologists an extensive coal bed lay under the channel and would be opened up by the tunnel. He denied that the promoters "ought a morroply (.1 the means of communication between England and France, and maintained that the Government could not consistendy oppose the bill now as they had permitted the preliminary works to be carried out. A.s a matter of fact the Govern- I ment were not unanimous on this question, for Lord it. I ' Grosvenor, one of the most important members of the Government, whose duty it was to keep them in ~rder—as he had done so well last night—(laughter)—sat on the Treasury bench representing another Channel Tunnel scheme as chairman of the company, whilst his colleague the President of the Board of Trade came down to 'oppose, the reject. All the mischief began with a letter }min Lord Wolscley, who was the first to raise the note of military alarm. Ho (Sir E. Watkin) now only asked the House to allow the completion of the experiment already begun, and to permit a state work to be accomplished by private enter- prise. Mr. CrisnaniaLmsr, in moving that the Bill be read a second time that day six montbs,eadmitted that many dis- tinguished persons in former times had seen no objection to

div.p: '1 Mt; EXAMINER S_AMURDAY, MAN 17, 1884.

this project. But that had nothing to do with the present question. It was only a few years ago—since he had been President of the Board of Trade—that he elicited the fact that there was a strong opinion against the scheme among military and naval authorities. A Committee of experts was appointed to consider by what means the tunnel could be rendered useless to an enemy in time of war, and the report of this Committee he regarded'as the death-warrant of the scheme. (Cheers.) They expressed the opinion that no human foresight could be relied on in every conceivable case, and the precautions they recommended were so com- plicated and so costly that if carried out the tunnel could never become a commercial success. They recommended that there should be a first-class fortress--which he supposed would have to be provided at the cost of the hon. Baronet and his shareholders—(laughter)—that there should be a portcullis, and means by which the passage might be closed on any occasion; that means should be provided for filling the tunnel with irrespirable gases letting in shingle if neces- sary, blowing it up. and flooding it. A joint committee of both Houses was afterwards appointed, and though they were noteenanimous a majority reported against the tunnel. The Government adopted their decision. He believed it would be the best and kindest thing to the hon. Baronet himself—though he would not thank him for saying so— and certainly to his shareholders, that this measure should new leave its coup de grace. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The debate Was continued at some length, most various opinions being expressed. The House divided :—For the second reading, 84; against, 222; majority against,l3B. THE CORNWALL SUNDAY CLOSING BILL. Mt. A. P. Vreaes mov,ed the second reading of the Sale of Intoxica- ting Liquors on Sundays (Cornwall) Bill. He said the feel- ing throughout the county in favour of Sunday closing was nearly universal. Eleven out of the thirteen members sup- ported the measure, and every single candidate at the last election promised if elected to vote for it.—Sir HENRY FLETCHER was opposed to Sunday closing for Cornwall, aud suggested that a general bill should be brought in.—Mr. WARTON opposed the bill on the round that it ought not to be in the -power of any majority to tyrannise over a minority however small. The hon. member protracted his remarks until a quarter to six o'clock, and so talked out the bill. MICCELLLNEOUS.—The Bankruptcy Frauds and Disabilities (Scotland) Bill passed through Committee. Sir J. Lub- bock brought in a bill to extend the Factory Acts te shops. The House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIIIRSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter past four o'clock. Cnatererae, Law AMENDMENT BILL.—The House having gone into Committee on the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, The 'Ear: of MtraaeoveN proposed to amend the second clause so as to limit the penalties for procuring women to , leave the United Kingdom for the purpose of leading an im- moral life to the case of girls under 21 years of age, so as to assimilate that part of the clause to the former part, which related to the offence of procuring girls to lead an immoral life within the kingdom.—The Earl of DALHOUSIE observed that it was not the opinion of their Lordships' Committee that there was no occasion for extending the proposed pro- tection to women over 21 years of age, and the amendment was negatived. A new clause, making it a misdemeanour, punishable with two years' imprisonment for a guardian or master to corrupt or attempt to corrupt a ward or servant under 18 years of age, was inserted on the motion of Lord NORTON—On the Bth clause, which empowered the police to take a woman into custody for loitering and importuning, the Earl of Dar- HOUSE proposed to substitute " soliciting" for "loitering," and carried his amendment by 38 votes to 25.—At the sug- gestion of Earl NELSON, the words "and importun- ing" were struck out.—The Earl of SHAFTESBURY moved the hasertiou of words bringing under the operation of the clause men who in thoroughfares or public places habitually or persistently solicited women or girls for immoral purposes. The Earl of Dautousin was sorry the Government could not accept the amendment.—The amendment was supported by the Earl of Aberdeen, Earl Cairns, the Earl, of Camper- down, the Bishop of Winchester, Lord Abardare, and the Bishop of Oxford, and opposed by the Earl .of Kimberley, Lord Carlingford, and Lord Balfour.—On a division it was carried by 34 votes to 20.—At the instpice of the Earl of Dalhousie all the provisions by which it was proposed to take powers for sending girls to reformatory schools or homes was struck out. The remaining clauses were agreed to, and the Bill, as amended, was ordered to be reported. The House adjourned at twenty-five minutes past nine o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS..---THURSDAY.

Bartlett that he did not think he was justi- fied in asking General Graham's opinions upon operations which in the opinion of the Government it was not desirable to undeetake.—The Pan ov MOISTER intimated that he pro- posed that the House should adjourn on Tuesday week for the Whitsuntide recess until the Thursday in the following week. The right hon. gentleman also stated that the Mer- chant Shipping Bill would be taken on Monday next. BUITOET PROPOSALS.—On the motion for going into Com- mittee of Ways and Means on the Budget proposals, Mr. MACFLRLANE raised a discussion upon the tobacco import duties, and moved that a revision of the present system of levying those duties is necessary, on the ground that although it is beneficial to the manufacturers it is detrimen- tal to the consumers.—The motion was opposed by the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, and was negatived with- out a division.—Mr. SLAGG urged that the time had arrived when the duties on gold and silver plate, and the system of compulsory hall marking of gold and silver wares should be abolished.-Mr. COURTNEY replied that owing to the general state of the finances the question must stand over for the pre- sent. If it could be shown that the application of the hall mark to fragile articles of Indian manufacture injured the delicacy of the work, a proposal that such articles, while still subject to Customs dues, should be relieved from the obligation of hall marking would probably be acceded to by the Government. Mr. MINTZ regretted that the recommendations of the Select Committee on Silver had not been more fully acted upon, and hoped that the time would soon come when the duty on silver would be repealed.—Mr. RTLANDS referred to the statement of the Chancellor of the Exchequer that he had been ezgeged in a careful examination of the different branches of expenditure and that be saw his way to considerable economies, and said the estimates which had been issued did not show any very great evidence of economy on the part of the Government. He hoped the Chancellor of the Exchequer would take this opportunity of stating in full what course the Government were going to take to bring about a reduction of expenditure. —Mr. Hicks and Mr. C. S. Read advocated a reduction in the charge for agricultural brewing licenses.—The CHAN- CELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Burnley, who bad been a consistent and powerful advocate of economy in public expenditure, the investigations made in pursuance of the views of the hon. member had already been productive of good results.— Mr. HEALY desired to call attention to certain rulings of the Speaker against the Irish members—lt was urged by Mr. GLADSTONE, whose argument was supported by Sir S. North- cots and others, that proper notice ought to be given of such an intention, and the Speaker himself upheld his con- tention. The Howe went into Committee of Ways and Means.— Discussion was continued by Mr. SALT and Colonel NOLAN, the latter of whom moved that the duty on tea should be threepence a pound instead of sixpence.—Mr. MaclvEn supported the amendment, and suggested increased duties on foreign winen and spirits.—The CHANCELLOR of the Ex- CHEQUER said the present duty on tea produced £4,400,000; and therefore if that were reduced by one-half there would be a deficit of about £2,000,000.—Mr. O'Suwvax remarked on the light duty upon champagne, which was the luxury of the rich.—Mr. IL B. MARTIN said he thought that the pro- posals of the hon. member for Birkenhead were Protection in disguise—After some further discussion,- the Committee divided—For the amendment, 19; against, 7C-51. The resolutions were then agreed to, and the House resumed. (Bankruptcy Frauds and Disabilities (Scotland) Bill WAS read a third time. The House adjourned at half-past one o'clock.

DURBAN, MONDAY, 7 P.M.—The following intelligence , has been received this evening respecting the movements of Mr. Oaborn i—On May sth he arrived at Inkaudhla, in order to protect the friendly natives from further molestation on the part of the Usutu leaders. On reaching Inkandhla he summoned the Usatu chiefs to appear before him to answer for their conduct, but they did not obey the summons, and continued their acts of hostility. On May 9th Mr. Osborn sent a force against them, which they attacked. The Usutus were, however, driven back. The loss on both sides was trifling. On the following morning a strong force, under Dalrulamanzi, made an attack upon the British Eel- dent's camp, but the assailants were repulsed with heavy loss. Mr. Osborn's losses were slight. The headquarters of the 91st Regiment have not, as was announced, been trans- ferred to the reserve, but remain at Pietermaritzburg. Two companies of the regiment have been ordered to Eltshowe, in order to relieve a detachment of the 41st Regiment eta-

USING BID LANGIIAGE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, 09 Saturday last, John Mosson and James 'Mason, of Hay- dock, were summoned for using language calculated to provoke a breach of the pease to Jane Wood.—Mr. A. Browne. of Warrington, appeared for the complainant, and M. L. Riley, of St. Helens, for the defendants, who pleaded not guilty.—The complainant is the, wife of Joseph Wood, a farmer, at Haydock, and they had been much annoyed by people coming on a private road gathering manure. On the occasion in question the complainant drove away a little sister of the defendants, and thereupon the latter came, and in the words of Mr. Browne, used ;‘‘ most disgusting, beastly, and abominable language" towards her.—They were both bound over to keep the peace. GOLBORNE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. LIVELY MEETING. The monthly meeting of the Golborne Parochial Com- mittee was held in Mr. Brewis's Office, Parkside Mills, on Wednesday afternoon, when there were present: Messrs. John Brewis, W. H. Arnott, John Fearns, I. Taylor, D. Gar- ton, T. Mitchell, W. Garton, John Unsworth, senr., J. Davies, R Yates, and C. S. Bennie (Surveyor.)—Mr. Ben- nie was elected to preside pro. UM. APPOINTMENT OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN.—The Surveyor, having stated that the first business was the ap- pointment of chairman and vice-chairman for the ensuing year, Mr. Wm. Garton moved that Mr. John Brewis be re- appointed chairman, and Mr. Wm. Mitchell vice-chairman, remarking that he did not think they could appoint better men.—Mr. W. H. Arnott seconded the motion.—Mr. Brewis observed that because they met in his office it did not follow that he should be appointed chairman. His ambitious days were over—(a laugh)—and if there was anyone whom they would rather have than himself he begged them not to ap- point him.— Lhe motion was then carried unanimously; after which Mr. Brawls returned thanks on behalf of himself and Mr. Mitchell, for the confidence they had replaced in them, and he hoped they. would be found worthy of it.

THE COMMITTEES.—The various committee; were next appointed as follows :—Lighting and Water: Messrs. W. • H. Arnott, T. MiThell, R Yates, John Davis, W. Garton, John Unsworth, senr.—Highways and Semerage: Messrs. W. H. Arnott. J. Fearns, I. Taylor. T. Pierpoint, D. Garton. Finance : Messrs. W. H. Arnott, John Fearns, J. Davis, J. Unsworth, senr. The chairmen of the committees were elected as follows : Mr. W. Garton (Lighting and Water); Mr. J. Fearns (Highways and Sewerage); Mr. W. H. Arnott (Finance.) ALLEGED ENCROACHMENTS ON THE HIGHWAY: A SCENE.—The question of the encroachment on the high- way in Heath-street by the erection of property by Mr. Unsworth again came up for discussion, and Mr. Unsworth asked if there was any difference between the property erected by him and that by Mr. Garton; and Mr. William Mitchell stated that there might not be, but two wrongs did not make one right—Mr. Unsworth: We have only taken in the ditch, and lam willing to pay for that. That is all lain willing to pay for.—Mr. W. Mitchell: It is a question of tight. If you bought the land for the fence you have gone beyond it.—Mr. Unsworth: We bought outside the fence.—Mr. William Mitchell; I say you did not.—Mr. Unsworth: Who did the ditch belong to 7—Mr. W. Mitchell: I saw the map made for it when it was said, and was the last bidder.—Mr. Unsworth: We have only kept in a line with other property.—Mr. W. Mitchell : If you have gene beyond the lies you bought that is another question.—The Chairmtn: It seems to me you bring a charge against Mr. Dnsworth of having built upon land which really did not belong to him.—Mr. W. Mitchell: It belongs to the high- way.—The Chairman: [think Mr. Unsworth is about one of the last men in the world who would try to take what did not belong to him.--Mr. W. Mitchell: Well, we cannot tell ahout that —The Chairman: It he has done so inadvertently I believe Mr. Unsworth would meet the committee in a con- ciliatory spirit and try to come to some satisfactory arrange- ment without any quarrelling.—Mr. Arnett: That is what ' has been done. Everything has been measured up.—Mr. Unsworth : You claim from the fence, and I am willing to pay for the ditch. That is all I have taken that belongs to the township.—The Chairman added that if the ditch was on a public highway he should sly it belonged to the high- way.—Mr. W. Garton: Yes, that is it.—Mr. Unsworth men- tioned other encroachments which had been made; and Mr. W. Mitchell added that the committee were now anxious to prevent any further encroachments in the future.—Mr. Unsworth said he did not wish to take a yard or an inch of the road that he had not paid for, but he con- sidered the hedge belonged to the field. If it was taken in and enclosed 40 years ago he did not see why an objection I should be "raked up" now.—Mr. W. Mitchell: This is a 1 new encroachment—Mr. Unsworth: I am not going beyond 1 that.—Mr. W. Mitchell : Mr. Fearns represents some of the land on the opposite side of the road, and he says if we allow Mr. Unsworth to go in on one side he shall claim the same right on the other.—Mr. Unsworth : That does not signify, if there is waste land on one side and not on the other—Mr. Arnett : But the law says that if there is waste land on one side it shall not all be taken in by one party, but equally divided.—Mr. W. Mitchell: I have tried to do all I can since the case came up to compromise the matte.r and settle it.— Mr. Unsworth : I am quite willing to pay for the ditch.— Mr. Foams said the committee had no personal feeling in the matter, and it was not a personal objection against Mr. Unsworth.—Mr. Unsworth remarked that it looked quite absurd on the face of it, that a street should be set out and then if he wished to make his fences lineable with the other property they should object to it.—Mr. Fearns : 'You have been at meetings yourself where it was decided that nothing ' further in the way of encroachments shocld be allowed, and I yet you are the very first to begin it.—Mr. Unsworth : I did it to make the property in a line with the rest. —Mr. W. Mitchell : Your only defence seems to be that because ether people have done it you are entitled to do it —Mr. Uns- worth : I will only pay for the ditch, and if that will not satisfy you you must do what you have done in other ques- tions.—Mr. Bennie (surveyor): What width would you call the ditch 7—Mr. Ueswortla : You must measure it and then you will know.—Mr. Bennie: It was filled up nearly all the way.—Mr. Unsworth: The ditch is there, and can be found. —Mr. Davis thought they had better be doing something definite about the matter.—Mr. W. Mitchell suggested that , if Mr. Unsworth would pay £lO as compensation for the en- croachment on the highway that the matter be settled at once.—Mr. Unsworth : I'll take the risk instead of paying ; £lo.—Mr. W. Mitchell: The only thing is then to put the lawyers working. Mr. Unsworth : Then you want a resolution that you pay the lawyers I out of your own pockets, and not with the ratepayers monev. —Mr. Arnett : It is for the benefit of the ratepayers —Mr. Unsworth : I say it is wrong that you ought te spend the ratepayers money in that way.—Mr. Arnott: I say it is not wrong.—Mr. Unsworth: I say it is wrong.—Mr. Arnott: I say II is not wrong.—Mr. Unsworth: But I say it is wrong. —Mr. Arnott: It is not —Mr. Unsworth : I say it is after counsel's opinion on the award. It is wrong if you throw the ratepayers money away.—Mr. Arnott: You should not take an advantage for yourself.--Mr. W. Mitchell: Counsel's opinion is that you have no right logo beyond the fence.— Mr. Unsworth: Counsel's opinion of the award is that it is not worth that much (twisting his finger and thumb) —Mr. Gorton : You are leading yourself astray on that point.— Mr. Bennie: We are only charging for an average of four feet.—Mr. Unsworth ; I have gone nowhere near four feet. —Mr. Bennie: What! have marked on the plan is strictly correct —Mr. Unsworth: I say it is not correct.—Mr. Ben- nie : I am prepared to take my oath that the plan is correct. —Mr. W. Gorton (to Mr. Unsworth): You will have to prove that it is not correct.--:The Chairman afterwards added that they were there to look after the interests of the rate- payers, and they should be honest to the trust reposed in them. They must do what was right.—Mr. Unsworth : This I thing has occurred in other parts of the township before.— , Mr. W. Mitchell: It has been decided at recent meetings ' that this thing must be put a stop to. and we are trying to put a stop to it —The Chairman did not see how they could settle the matter. It seemed as if Mr. Unsworth was charged with receiving stolen goods, by taking land that did not be- long to him.—Mr. Fearns: I think we shall have to take legal proceedings about it.—Mr. W. Garton: Let us go to law and test it.—Mr. Bennie : I am afraid we shall have to do that before we can settle it—The Chairman stated it was no good them coming there and wasting their time in dis- -1 bc eu sbs ei ns tg tao matterhave a otfe st th a et it ien, do. —n dM then h. eYna ttehset Tnh onutgt ehrt nito um.l. do would decided one way or another—The Chairman: I think we are in duty bound to do that —Mr. Arnott: his not a per- sonal matter for us; it is for the rights of the ratepayers.— It was afterwards unanimously decided that lea-al proceed- ings be instituted for the purpose of testing the rights of the township in regard to the award; and that the matter be placed in the hands of Mr. Mayhew, soficiter, Wigan. swocarso TRAOHDY tic BLECIIACKS.—A. shocking affair occurred at Weimer Barracks, Dover, on Monday. A ser- geant in the Royal Marines tamed Carr, entered the bed- room of his wife, who had recently been confined. He Wag only partially dressed, and carr44 his rifle and side arms with him. Before his wife had :Came to call for, help, he attacked her with the rifle. The poor woman tried to &- fend herself by putting her arms over her head, and in doing so had one of her fingers cut off. Rearing the woman scream several persons hurried to the 'room, but found tb, a corpse. Believlng his wife to be dead, an d bearing someone approachica„ be iqaded, his rifle, fastened a string to, the trigger, and fired it off with,' .f"4..":. ~ bullet passing through his head. ' At the incluont """ by 'Mr. Martin a verdict of "Temporary 'insanity " WU re- turned.

DaATTHROIJOII E—ICITEMENT.—Mr. W. T. Husbaucid deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Ham's Head Inn, Stubshaw Cross. Ashton-in-71 akerfield, on Tdesday, on the body of a collier named John Thomas, 58 years cf age, who resided at 12, Edge Green-street, Asbtn,acd w. it is state& died on Saturday in consequence (if being over ex- cited. It appears that the deceased had be...n suffering from excitement, and bad not worked for eight or nine months. He was attended by Dr. Hannah. Oo Friday night a woman who lived near him upset a paraffin oil lamp, and as her clothes caught fire in consequence she ran into the street. Deceased went to her assistance, and helped her husband to extinguish the flames, and the shock which he received hastened his death. The jury returned a verdict of death from natural causes.

PRESCOT. THE LATE MASTER OF THE WORKHOUSE.— "Vigilant,' the writer of weekly notes in the Walsall Free Press and South Staffordshire Advertiser, states in last week's issue of that journal .—" The election of Mr. Bicknell to be master of the Liverpool Workhouse is an event worth recording, Mkt Bicknell and 'Vigilant' were fellow pariah officers many years ago, and such was his ability and attention to duty that I predicted his 'rise' to the top of the parochial -ladder. The highest round is now almost reached. I offer my old friend my best salutations." PAROCHIAL RELIEF IN THE PRESCOT UNION. ac- lcordance with a resolution of the Board of Guardians a I printed list of the persons in receipt of relief for the half- year ended the 25th March last, has been issued for drools. don amongst the ratepayers of the townships comprising the Union, with the view of detecting and preventing ins- position. Any information respecting the circhmstances of those who have received relief from the rates likely to affect that end should be famished to Mr. Hartley, clerk to the. Guardians, all such information being treated as confidential. A summary of the amounts expended in relief in the vari- ous townships shows the following items :—Windle £737 69 2d, Widnes £5299s 3d, Sutton £834 16s 9d, Preacot £6BB • 108 sd, Bccleston £713 7s lid, total £3,503 10s 6d.

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

A fortnightly meeting of the Present Board of Guardians was held at the Union Workhouse, Winston, on Thursday forenoon, when there were present :—Mr. J. T. Hall (in the chair), the Revs. T. Chambers and J. Barnacle; Rev. Father ;T. Finegan Messrs. J. Newsome, J. Griffith, W. Birchen, ;J. Jackson, Matthews, J. Lowe, John Fidler, J. Leather- barrow, J. Buckley, W. Swift, H. Tuson, T. F. Hill, Wise. Tyrer, W. Gilbody, P. Loneton, J. Fisher, S. Mareh, W. B. Longton, and S. H. Hartley (clerk). THE PANTASAPH QUESTION: DEPUTATION TO THR BOARD—The C!erk read a letter he had received from Miss Williams, of the Pantasaph Orphanage. The writer stated that while fully admitting that the Guardians had certain powers, she could not on that account consider the proceed- logs which had taken place less harsh Sr unjust. She com- mended the benefits and advantages of the institutien to the notice of the Guardians, and asked that the metter might again receive • the careful consideration at their hands. He (the clerk) had also received a com- munication from Mr. Reynolds, of Woolton, who , had applied to the Guardiane to receive a deputation on the subject etating that he would accept the privilege offered by the Board. The letter concluded, "II the interview is not of a satisfactory character the whole question will be laid before the Local Government Board in London." ("Oh, oh ").—Mr. Fidler: It is a most in- jadicious letter. Mr. Newsome thought the Board ought not to stultify themselves by receiving a deputation if that threat wes to heng over their heads.—Mr. Fidler admitted it was a threat, bat he scarcely thought they should ignore the deputation owing to the indiscreet writing tof one gentleman -The deputation which consisted of Messrs. F. W. Reynolds, Sankey, JP., aud Harris (solicitor, Liver- pool.), was then called into the room.—The Chairman , stated that the Board would be glad to hear what the depu- tation had to say npcn the subject which had brought them to that meeting.—Mr. Harris then addressed the Guardians at considerable length, stating that they had not come there with any unfriendly or hostile feeling towards any of the Guardians, but solely as representative ratepayers and as repre- senting the interests of the Catholics in that neighbourhoed. He strongly maintained that children bad been removed from the Pantasaph in violation of good faith, although everything that was possible was done to benefit and im- prove them in every respect. He would even go so far as to say that the action of the Board in removing the children at se short a notice was studiously offensive, and he thought he cnuld detect a little tincture of religious feeling in it.— Mr. Fidler brought the letter written by Mr Reynolds before the deputation, and asked if there was not a threat c,nveyed in it —Mr. Reynolds explained that be did not intend it as a threat or intimidation, hut he just wished to intimate to the Guardians that the the matter might be referred to the Local Government Board.—The deputation afterwards retired, and the Rev. Father Finegan intimated that he would bring forward a resolution at the next meeting. THE MASTER'S REPORT.—The Clerk read the Workhouse Master's report, which showed there were 420 persons in the Workhouse, 43G in the preceding week, and 487 in the cor- responding week last year. Of the former number 263 were 'inmates of the hospieff. Teem had been 59 vegrtr.its re- he Clerk girls in lorkdale slicehvoeodl,s.and there were 182 boys and cGoNmATmIOunN stating that he had been appointed toaster of the Liverpool reandEasl icaOrtioTnlifErl°l3‘.4B°iTlek's3nei4ll (ArorkitTen'se master) i Union Workhouse, and he had to forward his resignatiqn as the master of the Prescot Workhouse. His wife also re- signed the post of matron.—The resignation was accented, and the Clerk was instructed to advertise for a new master and matron. THE ViCiNCY ON THE BOARD —On the motion o: Mr. Fidler, seconded by Mr. Tyrer, it was resolved that the usual steps b taken for filling the vactncy on the Board caused by the death of the late Mr. James Penketh. This was all the business of interest.

pRESCOT UNlON.—lhe Guardians of this Union are desirous of receiving applications from persons compe- tent to undertake the duties of MASTER and MATRON of the Workhouse. Candidates must be man and wife, prepared to enter upen their duties immediately on their appointment be- ing bacctioned by the Local Government Board, and the Master mutt be fully competent to keep the books ani accounts, and to perform the duties required by the Guardians and the Local -Government Board. The Matron must likewise be able to per- form all the duties required of her by the orders of the Local 'Government Board, and to superintend the domestic arrange- ments of the Workhouse. The saary of the Master will be £lOO and that of the Matron £6O per annum, with rations and furnished apartments. Printed form, upon whi..h applications must be made, can be obtained at these offices, or a form will be sent upon receipt of a stamped aedressed envelope of fools- cap size. The Master will be required to enter into a bond through a Guarantee Society for the rum of £2OO for the faith- ful petformance of his duties. SATURDAY, MAY 17, 1884.

LAST week we spoke of the quarrel be- tween the VICAR and his parishioners at St. John's Church, Earlestown, as being •‘ patched up ; " but it would seem that the patch does not quite cover the hole in the ecclesiastical gown. Through the arbitra- tion of Canon Hopwoon, the Rev. T. R. MATTHEWS got everything that he could ex- pect in the way of re-establishing his autho- rity; but he evidently wants something more; it is not sufficient that he must be recognised as master of the situation—those who have 3ffended him must humble themselves before him as servile slaves Acting upon the

agreement come to with Canon HoPwoon, he proceeded to arrange for Mr. DORMAN taking his place at the organ as usual on Sunday, promising to supply him in the ordinary way with list of hymns. But he had a second thought, and in his case " second thoughts" are not best; he afterwards sug- gested to the organist that he had better stop away for one Sunday, as he wished to have Canon HOPWOOD'S arbitration in hand be- fore doing anything further. What this meant was revealed in the following to his communication :—" If Mr. PEMBERTON is at liberty, I may ask him over next Sun- day." Mr. PEMBERTON, it should be ex- plained, is the Liverpool organist who was to take Mr. DußmAN's place, and what the VICAR was apparently aiming at was a break in continuity by way of showing the people of Earlestown that organist and choir must come and go just as he pleased. Mr. Dug" MAN, foreseeing another scene, remonstrated, and then the VICAR further showed his hand; he would not have the choir sitting in the chancel as usual—they must take seats in the ; body of the Church. That is to say, these parishioners, who had been giving their ser-, vices, were to be told by this paid servant Of Church and State that their conduct was not wholly to his liking, and they must therefore, , sit on the stool of repentance until it sheltie - please his reverence to say he could grant , them absolution. Canon HopwooD was al)" , pealed to, and he, we understand, while sur porting the authority of the VICAR, said he understood that the old organist and Choir were to take their accustomed places. rfh, choir—not being small boys to be told to or stand in a corner for misbehaviour —t°°, the matter in their own hands by occupYi% their usual seats in the Church; and if t"- Rev. T. R. MATTHEWS can profit by the experience which is said to teach fools even' there he will let them remain—thankful, aifte; "meddling and muddling," as he has done so many weeks, not that he can forgive then' but that they can forgive him. At Stockton Heath, near Warrington, the parishioners of the church with St. Thoula'r as the patron saint are, in a somewhat sil way, at issue with their vicar, the Rev. l uilas. 'his TOFTS. Mr. TIMSON, the organist in case is also the schoolmaster, and the vic-a having quarrelled with him he has receive notice of dismissal as school-teacher, net withstanding his having apologised for allYs offence he may have committed. It seerad peculiar, to the clergy of the Establisher Church that forgiveness with them is a rnatte,,, of preaching rather than practice, theh'e ! utterly deride in their daily conduct t"of teaching of the Master who spoke forgiveness " until seventy times sevea're It is not, we suppose, that they a , in themselves worse than otber they are given power and authori,_iis which no man ought to possess over P fellowmen, and they become by almost lint: perceptible degrees arrogant and intoleraflior They are the out-growth of a bad systen, we judge of the tree by its fruits. ROBERT DAVIES, who is one cf the Sco°ll, Managers at Stockton Heath, is good enollger as will be seen from a letter in anoth,..e column, to take a share upon himself of tP, burden of reproach, which weighs more Pard,. ticularly upon the vicar, in the dismissal () Mr. TIMSON. It is very kind of him, doubt, to endeavour to remove what lawYee, call the venue; but we prefer to pay soine,.l;9, gard in this matter to what Lord BEA-c°'ic, FIELD in his grandiloquent way once cha.l.-0 tensed as n the sublime instincts ol -se ancient people ;" and the people in this case are pretty unanimous in the conclusion t,i4„,c, have come to that if the Schoolmaster 11°4 not crossed the path of the Vicar the SchouA Managers would not have had a fault to fioti; is with him. We don't suppose Stockton Heath is an exception to the rule, and that it the Vicar to take the management of schools practically into his own hands. lallo deed, it is the usual thing for the clergY,Tny to speak of "my schools" and •‘ in teachers" as if noliody else had 3 1/01ce i a the matter. The Committee is simP and machine for registering his decrees, a is put in motion because the Governmn,e require a Committee and the Committee re; quire Government grant. But assuming tha the Stockton Heath Committee has be,) e; party to giving Mr. Timsos notice, that doe not get rid of the injustice, assuming iniugii , tice to have been done. There is no fa% found with him as organist, and, even if theo'f were, that is a matter beyond the province a School Management Committee; whileo to his qualifications as a teacher, the pare-be of the scholars, who may be supposed to fitting judges, are practically unanimous al appealing against his dismissal. They Pfbc the school pence, and are taxed for `r, Government grant, and ought not to be,oves. ridden, as they are being, by the Rev. I oj TOFTS. We venture to say that the Scllf, Managers, and we will not except "to; ROBERT DAVIES, Would be willing to-dayrk listen to the voice of the parishioners "kg withdraw the notice of dismissal, if the would give his consent. He may unforo nately be in a position to enforce his, °tel way in this instance, but it should be poll:he out that in matters relating to education .0 inhabitants of a parish are not so helplessrch, they are in matters relating to the Chit" oiv pure and simple. There is such a establishing a School Board, and if the trie"-,iitl rial of the people of Stockton Heath shi)-to be disregarded, we would advise theold, organise with a view to forming a, forthwith. It would be the means of get"i.-ge rid of irresponsible managers who, Inan-far matters, as in this case, so badly, and sO,l it as ,education at any rate is concerne,u,;o; would effectually disestablish the fallible r' of the Parish.

div.p: THE ExAmlNEtt sATURDAY, MAY 17, 1884.

not be a change for the better in the repre- sentation. Tenant farmers are slow to move, but they are moving and in the right direc- tion. They are beginning to see that if they are to have a fair chance in the world's race they must be less heavily handicapped, and are realising that. none of the weight will ever be taken off by the Tory party. The present Parliament has been too much ham- pered with Obstruction to permit of any great change in the land laws, and yet dis- tinct benefits have been conferred in dealing With ground game, and compensation for unexhausted improvements. The remedy f.or some of the ills from which they suffer IS not to be found in raising the price of meat to the working classes, who are the farmers' best customers, or in what is called relief of local taxation. The relief is no relief at all when it finds its way, as it usually does, into the pockets of landlords in the shape of increased rent. What is now Wanted is a thorough reform of the law of Primogeniture and entail, with increased facilities for the transfer and acquirement of land; and to this end tenant farmers in Cheshire and elsewhere should see to it at the polling-booth that they send such men to represent them in the House of Commons as Mr. LEADHAINI and Mr. RIGBY.

THE Parnsllites would have rejoiced, we suppose, if they had be,m successful in de- feating the Government this week on the Vote of Censure, thoupth we must, we believe, acquit Mr. r'ARNELL himself of such folly as his supporters displayed. He was a leader, however, in this instance whose followers we are given to understand, would not follow him. But what, it may be asked, have Irishmen to gain by playing into the hands I of the Tories ? They are at length on the eve of having justice done to them by such an extension of the franchise as, so far as voting iS concerned, will practically revolutionise the sister country. The cup is being offered to them, and they would—some of them at any rate—dash it to the ground. Perhaps they fondly imagined, on Wednesday morning, that the Tories would show themselves grate- ful to them for doing 'their level best" to I -turn out a Government which has done more for them in a single session than they have obtained from the Conservatives since Ireland was Ireland, not to say anything about demonstrating the absurdity of Lord SALIS- BURY'S gibe about the Government having, as he called it, " Squared the Irish." Well, if they laboured under any such delusion they are by this time undeceived ; the reward they have got fcr voting with the Tories is in the deliberate effort made last night in the House of Commons to deprive Irishmen of the bene- fits of the Franchise Bill. An amendment was moved by Mr. BRODRICK, and supported, be it noted, by Sir STAF.NORD NORTHCOTE, With the object of excluding Ireland from the Measure, and it was left for Mr. TREVELYAN. Mr. GLADSTONE, and other Liberals, to de- fend the just claims of Irishmen against the virulent attacks of the Opposition. We com- mend the debate to Irishmen of all sections, well persuaded that although there may be a number who are blind to the boons bestowed on them by the Liberal party,the bulk of them Will be quick to perceive that they have not merely nothing to gain; but that they have everything to lose by any such turn of Fortune's wheel as would bring the Con- seivatives again into power.

After the evening service the choir, assisted by several local vocalists, gave the sacred cantata "Victories of Judah," in 'elry creditable style. Mr, F. THE CHESHIRE SALT TRADE—An application of the London and North-Western Railway Company to repeal a clause in the Grand Railway Junction Act of 1833, came before a Select Committee of the House of Commons on Thursday. This clause prohibits the company from per- mitting manufacturers Is lay pipes along the railway in the Winsford district to connect pumping shafts with their works. The company propose to insert a new clause which Iwould give them power to grant this permission, but they - undertake that brine so conveyed should not be taken out of • the district for the purpose of manufacture either as salt or alkali. The particular case inquired into was that of Messrs. ' Yerdin and Sons, who have works in one place and pumping , shafts in another, and vet cannot convey the brine to the Place of manufacture. On the other side it was contended . that by conveying brine from one township to another a great injustice woutd be done to the ratepayers, and that aEI undue advantage would be conferred on those manufac- turers who happened to have works outside the Winsferd district. It was also stated that if the cliuse were repealed at Messrs. Verdin would be able to pump Winsford dry, and to lir transfer all the brine for the purposes of manufacture to • another district. Toe Committee decided that the case had not been made out.—The question of the costs o'. the peti- tioners was reserved. , THE VOTE OE CENSURE.—The following voted with tile minority in favour of the Vote of Censure on the Go- vernment in regard to General Gordon's mission :—Colonel ..; I. Thermo was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesday, to answer a charge of leaving his horse on the high- way at such a distance as Le be beyond his control. P.C. Holbrook said at a quarter to eight on the 2nd instant, he I saw the defeadsnt's horse without anyene in charge run- ning down Victoria-road.
