THE BiSHOP OF LIYEAPOOL ON THE House OF LORDS. —ln speaking at a luncheon in connection with the annual meeting of the Liverpool branch of the Church Missionary Society, the Bishop of Liverpool remarked that, to his own great inconvenience, as they were all probably aware, he was now obliged to be absent from his diocese a consider- able portion of the year. lie had every day to read prayers in the House of Lords. lie did not read them to a very large audience. He thought perhaps half a dozen made up the whole number; the prayers were over in abaut five minutes. He did not mean to say, however, that it should ;be done away with. He held that there was nothing like sticking to a principle. Some one had suggested that a chaplain should take that pace, but he could not help remembering that it would be one more step towards taking the bishops out of the House of Lords altogether, and if once that was dine people would ask what was the use of the Church of England being connected with the State at all. Therefore' ategreat inconvenience, he felt that he was doing a duty, but he hoped they would bear in mind that he was most unwilling, exceptfrom a sense of duty, to be away from the diocese. A RUNCORN FLATMAN AND HIS ROPES —At the Beaurnaris Police Court, on Wednesday, George Gandy, master of the flat Loto, of Runcorn, was charged with obstructing the highway by placing ropes across the sands at Llanfaes. The defendant admitted having endeavoured to moor his vessel by means of ropes. There was, he said, no place to moor a vessel in the neighbourhood, and, owing to stress of weather, he had been obliged to take ropes ashore, and secure them around a tree.—Mr. Massey (chairman of the Bench) said it was dangerous to allow roads to be obstructed by means of ropes.—The defendant: Yes, and it is dangerous for those on board ships if, after coming to roads, there are no places wherein vessels can be moored. I was obliged to take ropes ashore, as it was blowing hard, the vessel dragging her anchor and the crew being in danger of losing their lives. I hope that the corporation attending to the river will really en- deavour to do something in this matter, for protection is as much needed on sea as on land.—Mr. Massey hoped that something would be done in the way of finding mooring places, but it was not the proper thing to put ropes across the highway, and thus to imperil the lives of those travell- ing along it. As an example to others, the Bench inflicted upon the defendant a fine of 28 6d and costs. CURIOUS ROBBERY AT A WIDNES PTIBLIC•HOUSE.—John Mooney, a labourer, living at Appleton, was brought up be- fore Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junr. and Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes Police Court on Monday, charged with stealing the sum of 19s 9d belonging to John Davies.—Mary Davies said she was the wife of the prosecutor who was the landlord of the Queen's Arms Inn, Lugsdale, Widnes. At ten minutes Past one on Saturday afternoon the prisoner went into the tap- room and called for a pint of beer which she supplied. Ho did not pay for it, but she hid to change four half sover- eigns and a sovereign. She said " Who owns this sover- eign ?" an the prisoner replied "It's mine." She there- upon gave him 19s 93, and ha left the house in two or three minutes. She afterwards found out that the 19s 9d belonged to a man named Thomas Lewis. If the prisoner had not told her that the sovereign belonged to him she should not have given him the money. Patrick Ford deposed that he was in the public house at the time. He saw the sovereign in the prisoner's hand when Mrs. Davis gave him the beer, but he did not give her anything in payment for the liquor. I When he claimed the change and received it he had the sovereign in his hand. After some consideration the Bench tined the prisoner, who pleaded not guilty, in the sum of £3 and costs, or in default a month's imprisonment. Two YEARS OF MARRIED LIFE AT VITTON. Alexan- der Lowe, of Ditton, was summoned to Widnes Police Court on Wednesday, to answer a charge of assaulting his wife, Mary Lowe. He was represented by Mr. J. 0. Swift. Mrs. Lowe stated that at a quarter to three on Sunday the 11th inst., her husband had not come to his dinner, and she foand him engaged in a wrangle with three other men in the road. She told him it would look a great deal better of him if he would walk into the house and get his dinner. He replied that he would " make her pay ' for insulting him in the highway. She entered the house and he followed her. While she was sitting at the table feeding her baby he struck her on the head with his fist about a dozen times, and then struck the child. She screamed, and the neighbours entered the house, whereupon the defendant said she would " get more if she didn't get out." She therefore went to her brother's house. She had made up her mind not to live with him again, and she asked the Bench to grant her a separa- tion order.—ln answer to Mr. Swift, witness said the defen- dant had promised to pay her 108. per week for the support of herself and her child. She had been married two years, and she had suffered greatly during that time.—The Bench informed Mrs. Lowe they could not grant her request, but the case was adjourned for a month so that the parties might arrange a settlement. Runcorn( Union PROSECUTIONS. At Runccein Petty Sessiens, on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes and ,Mr. Henry Reynolds, Joseph Worrell, a labourer, was summoned by the Guardians of the Runcorn Union to show cause why he should not be committed to prison for disobeying an order of the magistrates made in 1879 to contribute towards the maintenance of his mother, whereby there was now £4 owing.—Mr. Houghton, collector to the Guardians, proved the making of the order.—The Bench ordered the defend- ant to pay the meney in 14 days, and informed him that if he did not do so it would end in his going to gaol.--Wm. Stanley was summoned under similar circumstances—Mr. Houghton stated on the 17th January, 1881, the defendant was ordered to contribute towards the support of his mother. Ellen Davies. He had, however, failed to pay me penny, and two distress warrants had been issued against him, but without result. Ile appeared before the court on the 24th March last, and the magistrates ordered him to pay £lO 17s. the sum owing, in 14 days. Seven weeks had elapsed since then, and no payment had been made, although the defend- ant was a furnaceman at Messrs. Golding, Davies, and Co.'s chemical works, Widnes, and earned plenty of money. He had no family whatever. Mr. Houghton asked the Bench to commit the defendant to gaol.—The Bench sentenced defendant to 14 days' imprisonment. A RAID ON WIDNES PUBLICANS —At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, before Mr. E. IC. Muspratt and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junr., Robert Smithson, of the Volunteer Arms, Lugsdale, was charged with having, on the 19th April, unlawfully sold, to the prejudice of Inspector Wood, three half-pints of whiskey which was not of the nature, substance, and quality demanded. Inspector Wood proved that the usual formalities bad been observed; and Supt. Barker put in the public analyst's certificate, which stated that the spirit was 33 degrees under proof, being 8 per cent. weaker than the amount allowed by the Amendment Act. Mr. Muspratt informed the defendant that he was liable to a penalty of £2O. The defendant explained that his wife bad mixed the seater with the spirit. Mr. Muspratt said the Bench would take into account that the was the defen- dant's first offence, and fined him £2 and costs £l. He advised him to take care that he was not again placed in a similar position. Defendant : I will fully well see that I don't offend again. The house is not worth keeping open,--Owen Tansey, of the Commercial Hotel, had sold the inspector a pint of rum, which the analyst certified was 36 degrees under proof, being 11 per cent weaker than the utmost limit allowed by the Amendment Act. Mr. Knowles, solicitor, who appeared for the defendant, informed the Bench that his client had been ill in bed for six weeks, and unable to attend to his business. His daughter had consequently mixed the rum and water, and had followed the directions of the spirit merchant and added three pints of water to half a gallon of rum. The defendant was fined £3 and Costs.—William Dodd, of the Riilwey Hotel, Victoria-road, was summoned for selling a pint of whiskey which was, ac- cording to the analyst's certificate, 38 degrees under proof, being 13 per cent. weaker than the utmost limit allowed by law. Defendant stated he had added water to the whiskey according to orders he had received from the brewer., Mr. Muspratt said he would have to amend his orders in future. A fine of £2 and costs LI was imposed.—Hannah Tarbock, Britannia Inn, Irwell-street, hail sold to the inspector a pint of rum, which the analyst certified was 46. degrees under proof, being 21k per cent, weaker than was permitted by the Amendment Act. Defendant was mulcted in a penalty of £4, including costs.—Jonathan F. Wade, the landlord of a licensed house in Page-lane, was convicted of selling a piut of whisky which was 53 degrees under proof, 28 per cent, too weak, and he was fined £3 and costs Zl. He explained that he had added water according to the instructions of his spirit merchant. —Petrick O'Loughlin, of the Star Inn, Elizabeth-street, was summoned for selling a pint of rum to Inspector Wood, which was 3 per cent. weakerithan the limit allowed by Act of Parliament. Mr. J. 0. Swift, who defended, calls I witnesses to prove that the defendant's daughter had ie idvertently added water to the jar contain- ing the rum, and did not inform the defendant until after the inspector's visit. In consideration that this was his first offence, and that the proportion of water was not so great as in the other cases, the Bench only fined the defen- dant £1 and costs £l.

BURGLARY AT RUNCORN.— A burglary was committed during Saturday night at the house of Mr. Thomas Kirk- ham, Waterloo-road. the thieves entered the house through the back window by removing a pane, of glass, and pro- ceeded to the different bedrooms without being heard. From etch room tnev brought clothing to the landing at the top of the stairs, and extracted the money from the pockets. James Hand- ley, W Whittaker, Id Coleburn, W H Rogerson, and W F &timid (Secretary.) He was also requested to get the notice boards re-lettered, and to obtain a new carpet for the Board-room. YOUTHFUL DEPRAVITY AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, before Captain Hazlehurst, Nathaniel Boswell, an umbrella repairer, and John Lewis, his step-son, 10 years of age, were brought up on remand charged with stealing and receiving knowing it to have been stolen, a purse containing 19a, the property of Mrs. Annie Besnett.—Evidence was given by the prosecutrix, P.C. Wallace, Henry Calver, Ellen Edmonds, Miss Wood- land, Mrs. Allaby, and T. Blease.—lt appeared that on Saturday evening Mrs. Basnett went into Mr. Fairhurst'e shop, Church-street, and mule a purchase which cost is. She handed a sovereign over the counter and received a half sovereign and 9e change. She placed this money in her purse, and the purse in a basket, which she put upon the counter. Whilst she was engaged, two assistants in the shop saw Lewis standing near the basket, and shortly after- wards the money and purse was missed. The same day Lewis banded his step-father a purse in Mrs. Allaby's lodg- ing-house, and Boswell then paid several shillings to Mrs. Allaby for his lodgings, although he had previously told her that be had had a very bad day, and only earned Is 26. On the Sunday he also took several men into the Royal Hotel and treated them to a " drink," giving Mr. Blease, the manager, a half-sovereign in payment. The missing purse was also found concealed in the closet of the lodging- house.—On this evidence the prisoners were committed to Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial. TETE DANGERS or RUNCORN BRIDGE.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Thomas Fay, a chemical labourer, at Widnes, was summoned to answer a charge of batting, on the 15th March, been on Runcorn Bridge in a state aif in- toxication contrary to the bye-laws of the London and North-Western Railway Company.—Mr. A. C. Preston pro- secuted on behalf of the company.—Evidence was given by Samuel Faulkner, 6, Cawdor-street, Thomas Blench, ticket collector at Runcorn end of the bridge; Gee. Barker, brick-setter, Lord-street, and Sergeant McMichael.—lt ap- peared that about nine o'clock on the night of the 15th March, he saw the prisoner ascending the slope at Widnes end of the bridge. He was in a drunken state, and on the bridge he attempted to strike a young lady who was ac- companied by a middle-aged gentleman. He was prevented I in his object by Faulkner. On arriving on the middle' girder of the bridge the defendant came "rushing along like a race horse," and kicked the gentleman twice. The de- fendant, when he got to the ticket office at Runcorn, was without hat, and lodged a complaint that a man had as- saulted him and taken his hat. He used language of a most abominable nature, and caused a large crowd to assemble, so that the entrance to the bridge was blocked until Sergeant McMichael and a constable appeared and removed the de- fendant.—Mr. Preston remarked that Runcorn Bridge was a dangerous place for a young lady to meet a drunken man at night; and he asked the Bench to inflict the full penalty.— The defendant admitted that be had had a few pints of beer, but denied the assault, and alleged that he himself was attacked on the bridge.—The Bench did not believe the defendant's story, and fined him £l, and costs, £1 ss. 6d.: total, £2 55. 66. ; or in default a month's imprisonment.— The fine was paid. MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR AT RUNCORN : SETTING A BED ON Flag—An affair of a most singular and mysterious descrip- tion occurre t on Monday night at the house of Mr. Elias Davies, St. Duke's Field, Runcorn. The family retired to rest about ten o'clock, the doors of the house being made secure as usual. About half-past eleven Mr. Davies beard a match struck, and in a few moments be was greatly alarmed to find the clothes of the bed on which he and his wife were reposing in flames. Be sprang up, and by rolling the bedclothes into a heap he Succeeded in extinguishing the fire. Naturally great excitement prevailed amongst the in- mates, but Mr. Davies states he heard someone run hur- riedly down the stairs and leave the house, and an examina- tion of the premises revealed the fact that a diabolical out- rage had been attempted by some malicious person or persons. The house had been entered by the kitchen win- dow, and several drawers and cuaboards in the kitchen had been ransacked, but nothing had bran stolen. On a table upstairs a bottle which had contained turpentine was found, the inflammable spirit having been poured upon the bed- clothes and set fire to. Beneath the bed a newspaper satu- rated with the same liquid was discovered, and near by an extinguished match was lying, thus showing that a moat determined attempt had been made to ignite the bed, and may be the building. No reason can be assigned for such a crime, and there is no clue whatever to the perpetrator. The affair has caused considerable commotion in the town. Mr. Davies' house was again entered on Wednesday night, after the fatally had retired to rest. The robbers had ob- tained ingress by removing the cellar grid, and departed by the back door, which they left open. Although they had evidently examined the cupboard where Mr. Davies usually keeps the rents he collects, they had only taken two pairs of shoes, and these were found on Thursday in the closet attached to the house. EXTRAORDINARY ASSAULT AT DITTON. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Thomas Evans, apparently a labourer, was sututnoned to answer a charge of assaulting Harriett Fletcher.—Mr. Knowles appeared for the complain- ant, and Mr. J. 0. Swift for the defendant.—The com- plainant is the Wife of Joseph Fletcher, and lives at ()Won. It was alleged that about nine o'clock on the evening of the 15th April she went to Fletcher's house and asked if "Joe " was in. Mrs. Fletcher replied that he was at the Clap Gate public-house, whereupon the defendant walked into the house, and putting his arm round her waist pulled her on to his knee and kissed her, asking her at the same time if she would be his wife if anything happened to her hus- band. She struggled away, but he again caught hold of her and repeated his conduct, and then tried to take indecent liberties with her. She told him she should inform her husband, and he begged her not to do so.—Mr. Swift cross- examined witness to show that the defendant was on familiar terms with her, and that she had often, when part- ing from him at the door, after he had been playing circle in the house' given him playful "digs in the ribs," &c- She said she did not scream when the defendant was assault- ing her.—Mr. Swift, in his address to the Bench, rem-irked upon the length of time that had elapsed from the date of the alleged offence and the proceedings being taken. There Was a well-known principle in the courts that in all cases of alleged indecent assault, the justices should not act upon the uncorroborated evidence of the plaintiff. No man would be safe if he Could be convicted upon the uncor- roborated statement of me women.—James Carogan, an en- ' gine driver, and Thomas Ireland, a labourer, were called, and stated that the defendant and Mrs. Fletcher were very friendly, and on the evening in question she asked him to go into the house. On Saturday night last, at the Clap Gate Hotel. Fletcher accused the defendant of inerelting his wife. Defendant denied the charge, and the two men then had a "fair stand-up fight '' in the yard, and after several rounds Fletcher acknowledged himself vanquished, and fetched his wife. She, in answer to his questions, denied that the defendant had insulted her.-Ihs Bench imposed a fine of 10s and costs.

Pickwell presided. The collections amounted to upwards of THE PROPOSED HOSPITAL FOR RUNCORN. There is every prospect that the present movement to establish an accident hospital at Runcorn will have a tangible result. The committee appointed by the Board of Commissioners to consider the question of ways and means have met this week, and Dr. Steele and Mr. W. Whittaker have been de- puted to endeavour to obtain promises of annual subscrip- tions towards the proposed institution. They have also, if possible, to Make arrangements with the various ministers of religion in tho town to hold a " hospital Sunday" at least once a year. Mr. Meadowcroft and Dr. Mounts, the medi- cal officer of health, have been appointed to look out for a suitable building for the hospital. THE BRUTAL OUTRAGE AT SPEKE.—JOSeph Gaiter, James Gaiter, George Woodier, George Guy, Wesley Yarwood, and Henry Johnson, all of Runcorn, who were found guilty on Monday last of maliciously maiming and wounding a heifer belonging to John Sutton, at Speke, in January last, were brought up for sentence at Liverpool Assizes on Wed- nesday —His Lordship said he was sorry to see young men such as themselves in the degrading and deeradod po3ition which they stood. He should not refer to the evidence on which they had been most properly convicted, because his observations would probably very little effect them, guilty as they were of a crime of this description; and they cer- tainly would be of no benefit to the public. If he thought it probable, or even possible, that another six young men should be found in this district capable of committing such an offence, he would express his opinions about the evidence. As he did not think that other men could be found capable of committing such an offence, it WAS unnecessary to say anything about the matter.—The prisoners were then each sentenced to eighteen calendar months' imprisonment. PRESENTATION TO A WIDNES MANAGER.— On Wednes- day evening a number of the workmen of the Mersey Cop- per works met at the Wellington Hotel, Widnes, the occa- sion being the presentation of a handsome seconds gold lever watch, made by Mr. G. Blackhurst, of Sankey-street, Warrington, to Mr. Thomas Shenton. The case of the watch bore the following inscription: "Presented to Mr. Thomas Shenton by the workmen of the Mersey Copper works, as a token of their respect on his leaving. April, 1884."—Mr. William Gandy presented the watch OR behalf of the men, and observed that although Mr. Shenton was severed from them, they would always be proud to meet with him, and they sincerely hoped he might long be spared to wear the watch.—Mr. Shenton said he could not find words to express his feelings en that occasion. During the time he had been at the Mersey Copper works he had always tried to act fairly to those who were under him, as the men would then always do justice both to him and the firm. He heartily thanked all who had subscribed to the present.— Mr. Shenton has been manager at the works for four years. TRESPASSING AT WESTON.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. W. Banks and Mr. Henry Reynolds, John Kelly and William Boyle were summoned on a charge of having, on the 4th May at Weston, unlawfully trespassed upon land in the occupation of William Griffith in search of game. The defendants pleaded guilty to trespassing, but not with the object of searching for game.—Joseph Griffith, nephew to the prosecutor, deposed that on the evening of the day in question, he saw the defendants and a dog by which they were accompanied, pursue a rabbit which jumped out of an hedge. They ran upon one of his uncle's fields, and although he shouted to them they did not re- turn.—Mr. Bankes said trespassing had become a perfect nuisance on Sundays and on weeknights at Weston. Men like the defendants seemed to think they had a roving com- mission to go on land and break down fences and hedges. It was only last Sunday that a lot of implements belonging to Mr. Griffiths were broken; and it was quite time a stop was put to such work. It WAS not for the gams for there was none on the place, but it was simply because they thought they could go on land and do any mischief what- ever. The defendants must clearly understand that they could not trespass upon land in future.—Each defendant was fined 20s and costs. MARRIAGE OF MISS CLARK, OF WESTON POINT.—The . marriage of Miss Kate Clark, second daughter of Captain • Clark, harbour-master, of Weston Point, to Captain , Edward William Whitfield, of Clovelly, Devonshire, only son of Captain Edward Whitfield, of the East India Service, wee solemnised at Runcorn Parish Church on Monday. Considerable interest was manifested in the event at Weston Point, and the Docks were gay with a profuse display of flags and bunting from the various vessels. The wedding , party was driven to Runcorn in two carriages supplied by Messrs. Yarwood and Son. The bride, who wore a brown

- velvet travelling dress with hat to match, was given away by her father, the bridesmaid being Miss Elizabeth Hillman Clark. Mr. Frederick William Clark acted as best man, and Mr. L. Rosenberg as groomsman. The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A., incumbent of Christ Church, Weston Point. On returning to Weston Point the guests sat down to breakfast at the residence of Captain Clark, and later in the day the newly-married couple left for Bristol. The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr. John Ashton presided, and there were present—The Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Lockwood, Messrs. Challoner, Aaron, Stokes, W. Whitlow' Jackson, Knowles, Dar'ayshire, E. Xallington, Weir, Mclntyre, Hamilton, C. Rigby, H. Lowe. Warlaurton, Pickering, H. Linaker (clerk). INFECTIOUS DISEASE AT WESTON.—.Dr. Adams, the medical officer of health, reported the following deaths from infectious disease in the Authority's district :—At Preston- on-th'-Hill, Lily Lyon, aged two years, from scarlet fever ; at Pritchard's-row, Weston, Richard Lightfoot, aged three years, from scarlet fever; at Ford's-terrace, Weston, William Ernest Norman, aged three years, from scarlet fever ; at Rose Cottage, near Lunt's-row, Weston, Ada Hibbert, aged seven years, daughter of Wm. Ilibbert, from " scarlatina (most probably) and dropsy." The first intimation he re- ceived of the existence of scarlet fever in this case was de- rived from the registrar's copy of the death certificate. At Acton Grange, Eliza Ball, aged three years and five months, from diphtheria. He received no notification of the disease , in this case. A COMPLAINT FROM THE CORONER.—The Clerk read a letter from Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner of the honour and fee of Halton, with reference to a house at Weston, lately occupied by William Podmore, upon whom he held an in- quest on the 6th instant, the jury were so struck with the condition of the house that they requested him to write to the Authority, and suggest that the inspector should visit the house to see whether it came within the province of the Authority to take steps to improve the condition of the house.—Mr. Farrington, the inspector, reported that be had , visited the house. The floor was in a shameful condition. The kitchen and back-kitchen floors were on the solid rock, and there were big holes in them. Some of the holes were 15 inches deep. How the people lived in the house without breaking their legs he did not know; but it was outside the province of the Authority to interfere with the alteration of the floor.—The Chairman: There is no nuisance, I sup- pose 2—Mr. Farrington : No, sir. The house is a rather tumble-down place, but there are a groat deal worse places. THREATENED ACTION FOR POLLUTION AT FRODSHAM.— Messrs. W. D. Jeans and Co., solicitors, Warrington, wrote as follows :—" We are instructed on behalf of Mr. Thomas Jones, of Pin Mill Brow, Overton, Frodaham, to direct your attention to the sewage matter which you and other persons have caused to flow through Mr. Jones's land, creating a nuisance, and polluting the water, and destroying the well upon his property. We understand that frequent complaints have been already made about this matter and unless steps be forthwith taken for the purpose of abating the nuisance procaedings will beat once taken in chancery against you and ether offending persons, for the purpose of obtaining an in- junction against the continuation of the nuisance." The communication was referred to the Frodsham Lordship

div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

. - Mr. John Ashton presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, when there were present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and J. Lockwood, Messrs. Challoner, Aaron, Stokes, Acton, Jackson, Whittaker, Campkin, W. Whitlow, C. Rigby, H. Lowe, Knowles, Darby- shire, Wallington, Pickering, Weir, Mclntyre, Hamilton, Warburton, and H. Linaker (clerk). Atr APPOINTMENT APPROVED.-1 letter was read from the Local Government Board approving of the appointment of Dr. F. S. Burnham as the medical officer of the Budworth district at a salary of £BO per annum. A GRATIFYING REPORT.—The annual report to the Local Government Board with reference to the operations of the Assessment Committee for the year ending April last was read. It stated that the railway property of the Union had been re-valued and resulted in an increase of £4,313 to the rateab,e value without appeals and litigation. Since the year 1871 the railway property in the Union bad been in- creased £15.949 rateable value, viz. :-1872, re-valuation by Corbett and Rigby, net increase £5,121; 1877, re-valuation by the clerk of committee, £6,515 ; 1883, re-valuation by clerk, £4,313. The committee had given special attention to the assessment of several works in the Union and had increased the assessment of alkali works by £1,284 rateable value; Frodsham gas works by £3O rateable value; and at a meeting of the committee held on the sth February, 1884, the clerk submitted a report of inspection and re-valuation of other works in the Union, showing a prospective increase of £770 rateable value. The total rateable value of the Union had been increased during the year by £5,738.— Several members expressed their satisfaction at the re- port. FINANCE.—Mr. Handley moved the adoption of the report of the Finance Committee, who had examined accounts amounting to £4l 139, and recommended them for pay- ment.—Mr. Mclntyre seconded.—Carried. THE SALARIES OF OFFICIALS.—In accordance with the notice he had given, Mr. Warburton moved that a return of theealaries and emoluments of the officials of the Union for the year ending March 3rd last, be made and a copy sup- plied to each member. He said it was desirable that the proportion of the Union funds spent in this direction should be known to the members of the Board.—The Clerk pointed out that the inf -rmation asked for was given in the half- yearly returns.—The Rev. J Lockwood considered the re- turn would be unnecessary work.—Mr. Acton seconded the motion, remarking that Mr. Warburton had taken a step in the right direction. He must say there was a good deal kept in the dark.—The Chairman: You must not say that. I think everything is conducted in a proper manner.—The Clerk: I must take exception to Mr. Acton saying anything has been kept in the dark.—Mr. Warburton: I don't for a moment suggest anything of the kind.—Mr. Acton: I beg pardon. Mr. Clerk.—Mr. Rigby could not see why they could not have this return without all this debate. They did not want to carry great " briefs " like the half-yearly returns in their pockets—they wanted a nice little bit of paper that would not take up much room; and then if any- thing turned ana they could refer to it.—Mr. Lowe sup- ported the motion.—Mr. Handley suggested that the return would be more complete if it contained a comparison with other Unions in the neighbourhood as to salaries. It would be more satisfactory to know what they paid, in proportion to other Unions.—Mr. Warburton thought they had acted on that line too long. They ought not to be guided by other Unions.—Mr. Handley thought the ratepayers would be batter satisfied if they knew how they stood in compari- son with other Unions, and he proposed an amendment that the return be amended by the addition of that information. —The amendment was seconded, and on being put to the meeting was supported by nine votes. Ten members voted for the original proposition, which was declared carried.

THE REPRESENTATION OF MID- CHESHIRE. SELECTION OF LIBERAL CANDIDATES. At a recent meeting of the Council of the Mid- Cheshire Liberal Association held at the Reform Club, Altrincham, Mr. I. S. Leadham, late Fellow of Brass- nose College, Oxford, was adopted as a candidate; and, at the urgent request of many tenant farmers who were present at, the meeting, a deputation was unani- mously appointed to wait upon Mr. Themes Rigby, of Sutton Weaver (secretary to the Royal Manchester, Liver- pool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society, and to the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture), and request ohm to place his services at the disposal of the constituency. The depu- tation, we are informed, met Mr. Rigby on Wednesday, and he consented to become a candidate at the next general election. He intimated, however, that in consequence of existing engagements he would be unable to take any part in political meetings during the present year. Mr. Leadham is a gentleman of considerable attainments as a speaker, and it will be remembered that at the last election he gave valuable assistance to Mr. Latham, who contested the division. He is a well known writer and has contributed interesting articles to the leading magazines. Mr. Rigby is a gentleman very widely known among the agriculturists of Cheshire, Lancasnire, and the northern counties. He was the son of a farmer living at Bewsey Hall, Warrington, and was barn on the 17th of February, 1830, thus now being 54- years of age. He was bound in 1845 apprentice to Mr. Wright, of Minshall, near Middle- wich. After serving his time, Mr. Rigby continued as a miller, and also made himself acquainted not only with theoretical, but practical farming. He afterwards became the owner of two corn mills, one at Sutton Weaver and the other at Darnhall. The latter is now worked by the son of Mr. Rigby, but the former is conducted by Mr. Rigby him- self with great success. He has a large business in the country round Frodsham and is helped by two sons of con- siderable business tact, SR that he is thus enabled to devote I a large portion of his time to matters of public importance. Since 1845 he has lived in Cheshire. Not only has Mr. Rigby a mill in the Middle division, but a large and well conducted farm, as well as another model farm at Darnhall. In addition to making himself acquainted with the most modern modes of husbandry he has practically ap- plied the knowledge he has acquired to all branches of farm work, and by his example he has given a healthy stimulus to agricultural improvement in Cheshire. In many ways has he manifested his interest in the tenant farmers. The , Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture, which was formed in 1868, originated largely owing to his efforts, and he has been ' the secretary of that most useful organisation since its foundation. He also took a leading part in the formation of the Over Agricultural Society, and he was likewise the secretary of this association until he was offered and ac- cepted the secretaryship of the Manchester and Liverpool Agricultural Society. He was on the council of the latter society for several years, and for seven years prior to 1871 he was a judge of farms for the society. In 1871 he was appointed secretary of the society, and he has held this posi- tion since to the great advantage of the society and the wide district in which its meetings are held, so that he has been for altogether 27 years connected with one of the prin- cipal agricultural associations in the kingdom. There are few gentlemen in the provinces who can speak with greater authority upon all questions affecting agriculture than Mr. Rigby, and therefore a batter and more practical candidate for the tenant farmers could not have been selected. He has written various articles, and has been a leading contributor to the Journal of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society for years. Many testimonies have been given by leading gentlemen in the provinces te the usefulness in 'Various ways ef the tenant farmers' candidate for Mid-Cheshire. Mr. Rgby has never obtruded his political convictions in the public offices he has held, and it may be said with strict accuracy that he has made no enemies in the society. He was urged to come forward as a candidate for Parlia- mentary honours two years ago, but he declined, though the calls of duty were very strongly placed before him by the tenant farmers. On being approached again on the matter a few weeks ago, Mr. Rigby gave no hopes of his consent- ing. It was more strongly pressed by a larger and even more representative body to come forward as a candidate as a matter of duty, and after some hesitation he manfully responded to it as a duty. There is little doubt he will mare the support of the tenant farmers and other voters in the division. Mr. Rigby stipulated in consenting to stand that he should not take part in any political meetings dur- ing the period of his official connection with the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society, and the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture. Until his terms of engagement with these societies have expired, he will maintain a position of strict neutrality, and it is pro- bable that he will not take a prominent part in political work in the division until a general election is imminent. In religion he is identified with the Congregational body, bat he is a Nonconformist of a moderate type. Though a sound Liberal, Mr. Rigby is temperate and moderate in his politics, and the attitude be assumes is rather calm and judicial than enthusiastic or impulsive. He is regarded as a very strong candidate indeed, and his rtturn to Parlia- ment, along witn his colleague, may be regarded with confi- dence.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, Tar RSDAY. I hasten to admit that my estimate made a week ago of the probable result of the division on the vote of censure fell short by twelve. With the Parnellites going with their accustomed allies I ventured to fix the Ministerial majority at " over 39," whereas it was only 2i. My estimate was made under the assumption—shared, I believe, up to the moment Mr. Gladstone sat down by every man in the House not being in the Cabinet—that the Premier would announce in definite terms the intention of the Government to des- patch an expedition for the relief of Gordon. Practically he took that course. When a Minister before Parliament and the nation solemnly declares that he is sensible of his responsibilities for the safety of a British agent and that he is prepared to meet them there does not seem anything more to say. But this Mr. Gladstone has raid betore and the House had made up its mind that on Monday he would make an advance in definiteness, and declare in so many words that as soon as the route was practicable a British force should be despatched. That that will be done is, f course, inevitable. With whatever opinion of the course adopted by General Gordon, and with whatever regret at the cost in blood and treasure, no agent of the British nation can be left in the desert vainly holding out his hands for rescue. But Mr. Gladstone would not put the phrases in the precise terms desired, and the Government majority fell off accordingly.

There is naturally, in Conservative clubs, a great cry of exultation over the diminished majority; Lilt after all, and in the circumstances hinted at above, it shows eight fewer men voting with their party, and some of these, to my pelt canal knowledge, were away simply because they were ill. Mr. John Bright, Sir A. Matheson, Sir Harry Verney, Mr. John Holms, Mr. Richardson, and Mr. Robertson who all voted with the Government in the last division on a vote of censure, are names one can run off on his fingers in counting up the absentees; all theee gentlemen are confined to their beds by sickness. That is half a dozen out of the eleven. The difference is largely accounted for by the more success- ful whip of the Conservative side. Of a total of 249 Con- servatives 239 voted, and five of the remaining eight were paired. in the Vote of Censure in February, the minority was 262, of which four were Liberals (for Mr. Marriott then Spired in the Liberal ranks), and 30 were Parnelites. The musters on both sides were extraerdinaly, the halt, and the lame, and the blind were brought in, and whilst Sir VVatkin Wynne was wheeled to the rescue of his party in a bath chair, Sir John Lubbock, like another Cnatham, hobbled on crutches into the division lobby to sustain toe Government. There was one exceedingly bad quarter of an hour for the Government. It happened between twenty minutes and five minutes to two in the morning. The Irish members had held their meeting at eleven o'clock, and at midnight Mr. Healy and others among them had diligently spread the report that they were going to vote in a body for the Government. This was unexpected zews for both sides. Lord Randolph Churchill load been in communication with both Mr. Sexton and Mr. Healey, and had reported to his party that he had 'squared the Irish." The news that they were going the other way was a staggerer both for the noble lord and Mr. Rowland Winn, who had been in his confidence. They fought against the conviction for some time, but were at last bound to give in. When the House was cleared the Irish members remained seated, two closely packed rows below the gangway, 32 votes at least, equal to a difference cf 64 on a division. That they should go with the Govern- ment was reasoriable enough. Mr. Gladstone, at some risk to his own popularity, had not only given them the Fran- chise Bill, but had promised that their numbers skould not be diminished on a redistribution of seats. This resolve had been bitterly denounced by the Conservatives, and would in forthcoming debates be staunchly fought against, If the Government were in peril, it meant above all peril to Ire- land, and the immediate loss of the Franchise Bill. These were circumstances under which even Mr. Biggar might feel himself nerved to resist the national tendency to "go against the Government." _ .

As the Irish members • remained seated chatting and chuckling whilst other benches were cleared a suspicion began to grow that some trick was in contemplation. With quick instinct members guessed that the Parnellites had been deliberately misleading the Liberals, lulling them into a sense of false security. It often happens in a debate like that which closed yesterday morning that for various reasons, sometimes sheer weariness and physical weakness, members will not wait for a division if they are quite certain that the Government is safe. With a solid vote of thirty- two a vote here and there was not of vital account. The Parnellites had carefully counted heads, and had come to the conclusion that if by their vote they could not actually throw out the Government, they woulrl reduce its majority to a point so narrow that a nominal victory would be an actual defeat. If by spreading the story that they were going to vote with the Government they could get away two or three Liberals the defection might just turn the scale. They had done iheir best in that direction, and with a childish love for dramatic effect, they kept up the mystery till the last moment. When all the benches were clear Mr. Parnell rose and walked out into the Opposition lobby, ac- companied by his pleased followers. Anxiety deepened as Lord Richard Grosvenor, fighting his way through the throng at the door, hurried up to the table with news of the Ministerial muster. It must in any case be a very dear thing and hope and fear lingered round the contingency that the Government bad lost the day. When the paper was handed to Lord Richard Grosvenor, in- dicating the victory, a bud cheer went up from the Liberal ranks, and when the figures were announced the cheers were renewed again and again. It was not only the satisfaction of winning the cLty but the delight at having defeated an unholy alliance, cemented by an act of the pettiest treachery. 'the majority, it is true, was only 28, but de- ducting the 32 Parnellite votes, which the most prejudiced Conservative cannot allege had the slightest reference to the merits of the question at issue, the real vote of the Rouse of Commons showed a majority of 60 in favour of the Government. The sudden and glorious burst of sunshine that came last Saturday, and lingered till Monday afternoon, when it dis- appeared in a thunderstorm, made a miraculous difference

in the appearance of London. People have not yet com- menced habitually to leave town from Saturday till Monday, and on Sunday the Park was worth a long journey to see. Tbe crowd was not so brilliant in hue as it generally is at this time of the year. Black is still commonly worn. Never-, theless a crowd of well-dressed people strolling in the sun- light under the thickening shade of the young trees is always a lively sight. As far as trees are concerned, Lon- don parks, always a week or two ahead of greenery else- where, are almost at their best. The lilac and the laburnam are now scenting the 'air in the very centre of the almost bouadlees population. In most of the parks bedding-out is now going forward, and in some is completed. I doa't know whether the painful impression produced by the so•called left-handed marriage of the Duke of Hesse on the very eve of the marriage of his daughter, will be re- moved by the intelligence that he has already cast off his newly-made wife. It is telegraphed from Berlin, to-day, that the marriage has been "legally dissolved." In the meantime the Grand Duke is a guest at Windsor Castle, and accompanies the Queen in her walks and drives; whence it would appear that the curious circumstances have been satis- factorily accounted for to Her Majesty. We know very little of the Grand Duke in England, but it happens just at this time that the publication of the letters of the Princese Alice bring his personality forward, touched with a loving hand. The last idea the Princess had in her mind when writing these letters was to limn herself. But she does this with an art the more perfect because absolutely unconscious, and the character drawn is so beautiful that everyone is in- aimed to resent whatever might seerrt a slight to her memory'. received explanation Yveniently found in the TofhtehceuorrreanntdlyureforketsedecamndducaLenisercaolnl allegation that his mind is unhinged. Mget his seat in Parliament too late to be able Mr. effectively with the pension of the Duke of Marlborough. His Grace, It is said, has eagerly listened to Btr o a ddl eaaulg h will one of Mr. Childers' financial propositions, and has com- muted his pension. Beyond this lump of ready money the Duke is eadeavouring to sell the family pictures, and on the whole, making things pleasan'. for the next heir. T'r; do him justice he is or.-ey fulfilling an intention always de- dared. There were some reproaches addressed to his late father because be turned into'vamey the matchless Sunder- land library. But the late Duke was fully aware that it was his heir's intention to sell the books and everything else in the house that could legally be brought to ilia hammer, and believing he could snake a better use of the money he anticipated him. Had he lived he would doubtless for the same reason have sold the pictures. Though it is not every week one has to chronicle such valuable pictures coming into the market as Landseer's "Monarch of the Glen," which occasioned such interest last week, there are still good sales in prospect, On

Christies walls, to be disposed of on Saturday, are several notable academy pictures of various dates. They include Mrs. Butler% "Remnants of an Army," Mr. J. C. Hook's "Kelp Burners; Shetland," "The Fishing Haven," and "Song and accompaniment ;" Mr. Brett's "Welsh Dragons" of last year, and his " Stronghold of the &limn, and the Camp of the Kittywake," painted in 1879. Mr. Colin Hunter's beautiful picture called the ' Island Harvest," Mr. P. Graham's "Rough Sea on the Scottish Coast," 1888, "A Chat round the Brasero "by John Phillip. Two paintings, " Changing Pastures" from the Hermon collec- tion ; and "Going to the Hayfield" by. David Cox, are also included in the four collections to be put under the hammer on the same Day.

The death of Mr. John Byrne, of the Mersittg Advertiser stair, removes a notable figure from the gallery of the Rouse Louis throne hroPremier of Francs by f our of Commons. Mr. Gladstone often speaks of his 50 years of public life, and people think with amazement of so long a pan. lßutip pe Byrnewas on beatthe th sat in the gallery with the old unreformed Parliaments when Lis phi .andyearWs.illiaßme IV. ruled England. He sat through and reported the events of Earl Grey's Ministry, of Lord Melbourne's, Sir Robert Peel's, Lord Palmerston's, Lord Derby's, Lord Aberdeea's, Lord Russell's, Mr. Gladstone's, and Mr. Disraeli's. He siw the Reform Bill brought in, slavery abolished, Queen Victoria enthroned, the electric telegraph at its first work, penny postage started. Fianklia embark on his last voyage, famine desolate Ireland, the Corn Laws abolished, geld dis- covered in Australia, the first wars in Afghanistan and Scinde, the Crimean war, and the Indian mutiny. Few men have lived so long, and fewer still have enjoyed such op- portunities of assisting at great events. Withal he was the gentlest, simplest, kindest-hearted man of his long day. In his youth he must have been a perfect Adonis. To the last he preserved his fresh colour, his bright eyes, his white teeth and his abundant hair, just silvered by the band of time that otherwise seemed to have fmgotten him. He died in his eighty-fourth year, as the immediate remelt of an ac- cident by which he broke his leg. There dit not seem nay other reason why he should die at all.
UNDENIABLE FACT.

THANKS TO THE PUBLIC. Sir,—Would you allow me through your valuable paper, on behalf of the labourers of White Cross and Rylands Bros., to thank the public for their kind support to them for the last ten weeks. The total amount of subscriptions re- ceived has been £169 7s, including £25 from Henry Thorn-1, ton, for which they heartily thank him, and hope it will not I soon be forgotten.—Yours, SAMUEL DUNBOBBIN. I

STOCKTOIsf HEATH PARISH. Sir,—With reference to your article of last Saturday, I feel bound, in fairness to the Vicar, to explain that what- ever has been done has been done by the unanimous action of the committee, of which he is ex-officio chairman, and that the churchwardens and managers (amongst whom I Humber myself) are equally responsible with him. Whoever communicated to you the information on which your article is based, ought to have informed you of this fact. If the base is weak everyone knows that the column must come down.—Yours truly, ROBERT DAVIES. Market-place, Warrington, 13th May, 1884.

Sir,—lf the paragraph on the above subject which appeared in The Examiner of Saturday last were allowed to pass un- challenged, it would lead to serious misapprehensien. May I, therefore, ask your permission for the insertion of the following remarks :—The writer has either wilfully misre- presented the case—which I should be loth to believe—or he has written in utter ignorance of facts. Neither vicar, choir, nor congregation is concerned in the way insinuated; neither are there any "strained relations" between the for- mer and the latter. It is insinuated that he vicar has sum- marily dismissed the sceoolmaster from his post for a very trivial offeece. This is totally untrue. The vicar has no power to do so. The dismissal was the unanimous decision of the school managers or trustees; and as the offices of schoolmaster and organist have always been combined, one dismissal followed the other as a natural course. Why a "lack of Christian charity" or a tone of "arbitrary supe- riority" should be imputed to the vicar I am at a loss to understand. Again, the paragraph professes to give a reason for the dismissal; and this it makes out to be a very trivial one. Now I do not want to say one word against the schoolmaster and organist, whose abilities no one I think can doubt; but your informant cannot be in earnest if he means to say that the managers had no more reason for their course of actihn than the one he quotes and make so very light of. The true explanation of that circumstance is very carefully veiled, and What had previously transpired is entirely overlooked or purposely omitted. The managers had good and cogent reasons for the course they have adopted, and your inform- ant will, by the course he has taken, only give publicity to that which the managers have, out of kindness to the official concerned, hitherto withheld. The paragraph then goes on to say that a protest, signed by 500 parishioners, has bten forwarded to the trustees of the schools, thus insinuating that the aid of these gentlemen had been invoked to counteract the assumed decision of the vicar. Why, Sir, the gentlemen this document was forwarded to were the very people who had decided upon the dismissal of the schoolmaster. Neither was the document a protest; had it been so I venture to assert that not one half the signatures would have been obtained. It simply bore testi- mony to the opinion entertained by the signatories, of the ability of the schoolmaster and organist, and modestly asked the trustees if possible to re-consider their decision. Many of the gentlemen on the Board of Managers are our leading townsmen, and I ask, therefore, is it likely they would arrive at their decision without good and sufficient reason? Will your informant also tell us how. many of the signatures appended to the memorial were those of chil- dren? How many were non-Churchmen? and, flow much vituperation and entreaty was expended in obtaining some of them? Now, Sir, I do most emphatically protest against the tone of the paragraph as an attempt to disturb the harmony which has hitherto existed in the parish, and to bespatter the vicar with unworthy imputations. I can only say that the vicar has the hearty sympathy of his congregation under the unmerited pain whiclithis paragraph has caused him. .
Apologising for my trespass, I am, yours respectfully, ,A PARISHIONER.

CHURCH DISPUTE AT STOCKTON HEATH. Sir.—Under the above heading I obse,ved in your issue of Saturday last, an article having reference not so much to a church dispute in the ordinary acceptation of that phrase ' (so I consider after a c Ireful perusal) sea grievance between ; the vicar and the master of the church schools, and I cannot but think that many readers of your paper will incline to the belief that surely there must be something considerably more grievous (although I have every reason to believe such is not the case), than that to which the article refers; as. braid of managers would be so blind to justice as MU/ well ttlel 'servant Inieapee of the trivial lamtter in qfflrtioth and tile vicar should be the 'last One to so Keck. lerly !nen that greatest of all Chriatian gre.tes " charity " as to turn a deaf ear to any expression Of tonrrition, and use no means whatever to persuade the managers to reconsider their decision. This, however, has it appear yet to be done (for a most humbly written apology was tendered) and time having passed without any aembl.mce of the matter being as it were reinstated, and the position of organist was, I be- lieve, advertised prior to any notice being given, it was felt by many that an injustice was being done, and with a feel- ing of sympathy for Mr. Timson, some of the choir and con- gregation drew up a most respectful petition asking the managers kindly to reconsider their decision. In three days they procured some 510 signatures to it from those parents whose children attend the school members of the cong ' ,egation and the choir as a body. A copy of the petition was duly forwarded to each of the managers, ane„ although it has been in their hands many days, nothing-further has been heard, save that rumour says a manager (a gentleman one would presume terribly afraid of sacrificing his dignity) expressed his opinion that the petition constituted "the greatest insult which could have been offered the managers.' This indeed is sad to think of, especially in this age of advancement when so many of our well-to-do neighbours profess to be such heroes in the cause of social rights, and yet a petition containing over 500 sig- natures (this representing nearly the whole of the adult population at the parish), many of them those of our local and influential business men, is apparently shelved and treated with cool indifference. It would thus appear that the parishioners' voices most be silenced, their petition ig- nored, and they to be treated as those who have no right to ' interfere (although actuated by feelings of keen sympathy) on behalf of oce, who, to say the least," is being somewhat harshly dealt with. It cannot, I think. be questioned that the congregation have a right to be heard, for, as supporters of the church and its living, it is treating thorn discour- teously, and certainly unchristianlike, by allowing a most respectful petition to receive, as it seems, no consideration. Probably the result, even yet, may be favourable for the one whose cause they thus champion, but the prospect is gloomy; however, we may, I trust, hope that the matter will, in some way or another, force upon those concerned the consideration that it is only right they should endeavour to exercise some compassion for a faithful and hard-working servant. "Humanum est errare."/ Apologising for trespassing on your space, I am. yours faithfully, JUSTITIA.
GREEN-ALL ROUND.

Sir,—l see the "old man" in-" eloquent " has been at it again, and again he has given his hearers another specimen of his utter inaptituJe for the poet he so foolishly dares to hope for. It lea matter of amusing speculation to me what the monist eendition of this brilliant sample of a political candidate ewe be. Does he think himself a representative man? I think he would be a very good member for War- rington; if it wereinhabited chiefly by imbs.ciles. But as the representative ;of a somewhat important commercial community he is or would be utterly, out of place. And it is a pity; he cannot be brought to eee this. It would save the poor old man a world of " bother" would he but see how void of hope his chances are, and how he is but lured to certain disappointment by interested " friends," and his ' own foolish and misplaced ambition. He poses as the ; "friend of the workingman!" Was it in this capacity he ' closed public footpaths in order to preserve game ? I re. i gard the man who does this as no friend to the public, but as a public nuisance. The workingman for sooth ! Why if this seedy politician and his party had been allowed to have ] their own way the artizans would have been effectually ] gagged. No votes for them! If there really be such a /taus nature as a real live "Conservative workingman "let him consider these propositions:—He now enjoys the privilege 1 of a voice in the selection of a representative in Parliament. Does he value this privilege? Did Hilbert Oreenall agitate to obtain for him this boon? Is he doing so now to obtain it for such of them as may happen to reside outside the borough boundary ? LA them think of this the next time they are entreated to attend a ward meeting there to "open I their mouths and shut their eyes and see what 'Gilbert' I sends them." If the people of Warrington consider them- 1 selves to be "duffers" Sir U. Greenall would be a very fit representative for them.—l am, &c., JOHN PEERS. ! Penketh, 12th May, 1884.

THE TORIES AND THE WIRE TRADE. Sir,—l wonder if our local Tories ever read the newspapers. If so, they must be aware that as a united body they have ceased to exist, at least Her Majesty has no longer a loyal Opposition. As a Radical, I, for one, am heartily sorry this is so. The stronger the Opposition the more "go " will the Government have. While Lord Randolph hungers after the Birmingham caucus, my Lord of Salisbury insists that the power shall be in his hands, and a very pretty quarrel they make of it, while all theworld wonders. Judging from the speeches made at the latest Conservative meeting, I should say there is a special bit of " choosing " going on. Sir Gilbert had better not meddle with coining words; his success lies in another direction. No one in Warrington is being more " choused " than he is, and this by his " dear " friends. I notice Alderman Kean has some- thing to say about the Conservatives being united and the Liberals disunited. Poor fellow, like the ostrich, he refuses to see his danger, believing that "ignorance is bliss," hut most remarkable of all is the following passage: "If the i wire manufacturers of Warrington had all been Tories, they would have been branded as grinding the workmen to death. He was glad to say that where Conservative capital was in- vested the people were getting good money." Sir, this pas- sage is all humbug, intended to "choose" the people. In the struggle the wiredrawers have been engaged in the worst employer the men have had to deal with is a Tory, and head manager of White Cross, and be has given the keenest blow to the trade it ever had. Another wire mill, Longford Bridge, is carried en by Tory money, and all the labour is of a kind known as " knobstick," and the head of which is Sir Gilbert. Let us have the truth, Alderman Kean, and, when you have time, let us snow, in our own town, one place carried on by Conservative capital where the men get "good money." If you cannot do this, suffer yourself to be snuffed out by CLIFFORD DIX. May 12th, 1884.

QUARREL BETWEEN WOMEN.—At the Newton Petty Ses- sions on Saturday last, Elizabeth Carlin was summoned for assaulting Catheiine Rogers, at Earlestown, on the 26th April.—The complainant stated that the defendant had used very abusive language to her, and also spat in her face. When she asked her what she had done it for, she replied that she would have her life.—Several witnesses were called after hearing whom the Bench said they considered the case proved, and fined the defendant 101. and costs.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE AT DURTONWOOD.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, several cases of neglecting to send children to school were heard. The prosecutor was Mr. Forster, School Attendance Officer. The following were each fined ss. :—Edwin Williamson, Samuel Lloyd, Robert Fairclough, John Corvin, John Martin, and John Hill. Fines of 2s. 6d. were imposed upon John Carr and William Travers, and the following cases were adjourned :—Mary Hopkins, James Millington, Thomas Molyneux, Charles Pennington, and Charles Rothwell. A COMING-OF-AGE TREAT AT EARLESTOWN.—The school children, numbering nearly 250, attending the Catholic Schools, Crow-lane, were kindly entertained to tea in St. Mary's Hall on Saturday evening last by Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Forster, of Earlestown, as a celebration of the corn- ing of age of their son, Mr. James Henry Forster. The tea was an excellent one, and the children highly appreciated the kindness and generosity of Mr. and Mrs. Forster. The children afterwards amused themselves in various ways, and were each presented with an orange. CHIMNEY FIRING AT THE VULCAN.—CAUTION.—At the Newton Petty Sessions OR Saturday last, James Baker, resid- ing in Vulcan cottages, was summoned for allowing the chimney of his dwelling to be on fire on the 26th ult.—P.C. McMullen stated that the Vulcan Foundry Company had made several complaints about the tenants setting their cot- tage chimnies on fire; especially when the constables were away at the sessions. Witness was on duty in plain clothes on the date ha question, and he caught some of the parties who were guilty of it. The defendant was fined 35., includ- ing costs.--A like penalty was imposed en John Gregson for a similar offence on the sth inst.

SINGULAR DEATH OF A BM—Ellis Ogden, 13 years of age, son of George Ogden, residing in Fairclough-street, Earlestown, died under somewhat peculiar circumstances on Tuesday morning. It was rumoured in tbe neighbourhood that the lad had been accidently poisoned by " sucking " small twigs, in order to get the bark off when making "whistles," and there certainly appeared to be some foun- dation for the report. On Sunday last, the deceased did make several whistles, and on that evening he complained of feeling unwell. He became sick and vomited, and was much worse on the Monday morning. He iernained in a semi- conscious state throughout the day, and Dr. Handyside was sent for. Notwithstanding all efforts, however, the lad rapidly grew worse, and expired at seven o'clock on Tues- day morning. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNITERSARY.—The anni- versary services in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Sunday School, Cross-lane, Earlestown, were held on Sun- day last, and were of an encouraging character. The preacher both morning and evening was the Rev. J. M. Fair. bourn, resident minister, whose addresses were listened to with the greatest attention. The chapel was crowded in the afternoon, when a sacred cantata entitled " The choicest gift " was given by the choir, assisted by a number of the scholars and a few friends. The 9010 parts by Miss Sydes, Miss Swann, Mr. S. Swann, Mr. Gilmour, Mr. Gibson, and Mr. Willis were well rendered. At each of the services special hymns were sung. The choir was under the leader- ship of Mr. H. Parr, and Miss E. L. Greenall presided at the harmonium. The collections realised over £53, a sum in advance of that of last year. FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTIONS: AN EARLESTOWN TRADESBAN Sperseemen.-Before Colonel McCorquedale, R. Houghton,T. J. Gillespie, C.Pilkington, and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqs., at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, Matthew Win- staniey, a greengrocer, in Bridge-street, Earlestown, was summoned for obstructing the footpath with two hampers on the sth inst —The defendant pleaded not guilty to ob- structing the footpath.—P.O. Lloyd deposed that he saw two hampers containing cabbage on the footpath opposite the defendant's shop. A great many complaints had been made about greengroCets obstructing the footpath and they had all been warned About it. In reply to defendant, wit- ness added that the hamper was about one foot on the footpath over the kerbstone. The footpath was eight feet wide. He saw it there from six o'clock until half-past sevea.—The chairman said the Bench had considered the case and would dismiss it if the defendant would promise to pay the costs. The police were quite right in keeping the streets and footpaths quite clear; and the Bench had no doubt it would be sufficient warning to the defendant and others.—The defendant promised to pay the costs and re- marked that he had not had any intention of breaking the law; but he did not see why other people should be allowed to offend in a similar way and he be summoned for it. EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT FOOTBALL CITALLENGE Cur: FINAL TrE.—The final tie of the Earlestown and District Football Junior Challenge Cup competition was played at Wargrave Moss on Saturday afternoon, the 4ompeting teams being the Newton St. Peter's and Earlestown Wanderers' menu. Throughout the preceding week much interest was I centred in the match, and a considerable amount of money was staked upon the result. The Wanderers were the "favourites "—in fact SO much so that the only question with many of their supporters was as to how many goals they would win by. But a surprise was in store for the spectators, who numbered several hundreds, the weather be- ing beautifully tine. In the first half the Wanderers played down bill, but it was at once seen that the game was net go- ing to be the runaway affair for that eleven as their sup- porters expected.. -11 c. New:onions played..up remarkable „ . . .•

well, and in this half, though playing up hill, they had the best of the game. At half-time the score was—Newton, one goal; Wanderers, hone. On the change of ends the New. , tonians had the ground in their favour, and they severely pressed their opponents throughout. The latter never had a chance to score, while Newton added ether three goals, and thp cleverijr won by four goals to none. They were heartily Cheered on leaving the field. The Newton St. Peter's team and their supporters afterwards gathered at the Sunbeam Inn, Wargrave, where, amid much enthusiasm, handsome silver medals were presented to the winners by Mr. P. 'births, (chairman of the Earlestown Association Club). Each member of the team on coming forward to receive his medal was well applauded. The toasts of "New- ton St. Peter's Club," " The,Barlestpwn Association Club," "The Referee (Mr. P. Hastie)," and "The Secretary (Mr. J. Daxbury,", were warmly received and responded to. EARLESTQWN GOSPEL Missrox.—The temperance workers conducting the Gospel Mission in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestows, held a public meeting on Tuesday evening, when Mrs. Caroline John, of Bolton, a well known tem- peranee worker, gave an instructive and interesting address on the drink question. The friends met in the Market- square about seven o'clock and alters hearty invitation bad been extended to those gathered round to attend the meeting in the Co-operative Hall, a procession was formed and marched to the hall. Here there was a very large attend- ance, and Mr. John Prescott, who presided, was supported by Mr. John Clarke and Mr. Joseph Cordingley, in addition to Mrs. John. The Chairman, in introducing Mrs. John, , remarked that so much injury and crime was occasioned in the nation through the chick that that was a sufficient rea- son why a,wooran should stand upon a platform to advocate the cause of temperance. (Applause.)—Mrs. John then rose to address the meeting and was very warmly received. She pointed out that men Of all classes were being slain by the drink, and went on to allude to thki(ifforto which were being made to suppress it. She said titre had got a Sunday Closing Bill for Scotland and Wales, and what was wanted was a Sunday Closing ' Bill for England. They were anxious for it and would have it. Speaking of moderate drinkers, she said that those who even drank in moderation • were upholding that awful system which was causing the most terrible crimes to be committed in the country that evet debased the history of any coun- try. The people of the country spent six million pounds more money in drink every year than the amount of all the rents in the United Kingdom. Altogether £160,000,000 were expended in the drink traffic, and yet they cried out about bad trade. If they wanted good and better trade they must strike a blow against the drink; and if they individually ranted plenty of good work and good wages they must sign the pledge and stick to it. (Applause.)— The choir, under the leadership of Mr. Barcroft, gave a selection of music, Mr. S. Birks presiding at the harmo- nium. At the close of the meeting about 30 persons signed the pledge. DEATH OF A FARM LAMM:HIER AT BERTONWOOD.-011 Wednesday afternoon Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Chapel House Inn, Bartonwood; on the body of John Massey, 5,5 years of age, a farm labourer in the employ of Mrs. Kllshaw, who occupies a farm at Burtonwood. The following' evidence was given :—Sarah Margaretta: Massey deposed that the deceased. was her hus- band, and lived in Tan House-lane, Buttonwood. He was 'a farm labourer at Mrs. Kilshaw's farm. She saw him alive on Saturday morning last, when he left for his work. At nine o'clock the same night she heard of his death.—Mary Ellen Pratt stated that Mrs. Kilabaw was her mother, and she lived at her house. John Massey was oce of her mother's labourers. At half-past seven o'clock on Saturday night she last saw him alive, when he was bringing some water from the pump. She spoke to him. He was quite sober, and was a good workman. They missed him about eight o'clock, when they usually finished off work. As the de- ceased did not come in the house, witness and her sister went to look for him. They searched about the premises, but did not go into the stackyard. The other farm labourers had gone to Warrington or Bariestown, and 'no one was in the house exe4pt witness and her sister. At twenty minutes; past nine her brother Albert returned, and they told him that Massey had not come in • for -this Pay, and , he went • and searched for him. He found him in the stacki-ard about ten minutes later—Albert Kilshaw, the brother to last witness, said he was the manager of the •farm for his mother. When he returned home on ,paturday night he went to leek for Massey, after what his sister told him. He found him behind a cart in the stackyard, lying on the ground. The cart. was filled with straw. He would be about two yards from a stack of straw. A ladder wag lying in the opposite direction to that in which the deceased was lying. He thoughrthe deceased in going up the lad- der to gat on the straw, td cover it with a tar sheet, must have fallen, and in falling kicked the ladder over. The tar sheet was on the deceased's legs. Deceased had a felt hat on, which had been knocked over his head and face,shewing that he bad alighted on his head. His nose was a little scarred. The body was quite cold, and witness immediately sent for P.C. Grundy.—The Deputy-Coroner, in summing up, briefly remarked that from the evidence it appeared that the deceased had fallen from the ladder, and alighting on his head. had been killed instantaneously. He thought they could only return a verdict of accidental death.—The jury then returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

EIIMANUEL CITURCH, WARRINGTON- On Tuesday evening an ordination service was held in Emmanuel Church, Bold-street, by the Right Rev. T. H. Gregg, D.D., Bishop of Vernlam. There was a moderate congregation. In addition to the Bishop the following clergymen were present and took part in the service :—The Rev. G. J. Lacell, rector of Christ Church, Hemel, Hemp- stead ; the Rev. Charles Snosswell, vicar of Christ Church, Braintree; the Rev. W Titherington, Emmanuel Church, Chester; and the Rev. W. Mules, of Warrington. After the singing of hymns and the reading of the service, a sermon, which was attentively listened to, was preached by the Rev. G. J. lateen, who took for his text the 11th verse of the Beh chap. of the Song of Solomon, " I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished, and the promegranates budded." In concluding his sermon the reverend gentleman said they were called together that evening for no light matter. It was a matter of solemn responsibility. It was a solemn responsibility for the chief pastor and for those who assisted him in the laying on of hands. It was a solemn thing for them to be witnesses of that service, and he prayed that they would send up their prayers and supplications to the throne above for an abundant blessing on those services. It would be useless for him, a comparative stranger, to speak in the presence of their presbyter. The beautiful building in which thery were gathered bore testimony to the way he had laboured, nobly assisted by some who were present, which was stronger testimony than any he could bear to his fitness for the work. He advised the new presbyter to preach the Gospel, live the Gospel, and let his whole life proclaim to his fellow-men that he believed, in what he preached, and that the Gospel was a reality to him. In conclusion, Mr. Lacell advised the congregation to pray for and assist their minister. After the sermon the Holy Communion was administered to the whole of the congre- gation. On the following day the Rev. William Mules was installed as vicar of Emmanuel Church by the Right Rev. Bishop Gregg. There was a good congregation. The sermon was preached by the Rev. Charles Snosswell, A.K.C., vicar of Christ Church, Braintree, from the text Jeremiah, 23 c., 28 v.:" He that hath My word let him speak My word : faithfully." The lessons were read by the Rev. G. J. Lacell, and the services by the Rev. W. Mules.
