THE .EARLESTOWN CHURCH DISPUTE.—THE VICAR AND THE CHOIR. The an louncement which was made last week that the dispute at St. John's Church, Earlestown, had been amic- ably settled by the arbitration of the Rev. Canoe Hopwood, of Winwick, and that peace WAS once more to reign in the recently much disturbed parish of St. John's, seems to have been somewhat premature, judging from the reported pro- ceedings of last week end. As our readers will be aware, the interview with Canon Hopwood Was apparently con- cluded in a perfectly friendly manner; all shook hands ' and parted, as was thought, the best of friends. The rev. Canon expressed the hope that a perfect reconciliation had been come to, that bygones would be bygones, and that in future everything would go on peaceably and quiet. This also seemed to be the wish and hope of every parishioner, but facts have turned out to be different to the anticipations. However, on the Thursday night after the interview, Mr. Durman (the organist) was informed by the Vicar, by ; means of a letter, that he would be glad to have an inter- view with him as early as possible. Mr. Durman waited upon the Vicar on the following day as to the future ser- vices, and the Vicar subsequently added that if Mr. Dorman would call in the evening he should have the list of hymns for the following Sunday given to him. But when Mr. Darman called at the Vicarage in the evening, instead of receiving the list of hymns in accordance with the Vicar's promise, he had the following note handed to him :—" The Vicarage, Earlestown, oth May. Dear sir,—After seeing you this morning, and having had an interview with Canon Whitley, I think it would behest to have Canon Hopwood's arbitration in hand before we do anything further, and have, therefore, decided to wait until Sunday week and give notice next Sunday. In that case would it not be best for your own feelings that you should be absent next Sunday, as I may refer to the new arrangements.—Yours faithfully, T. It. MeTTunws.—P.S. If Mr. Pemberton is at liberty I may ask him over next Sueday." After receiving this let- ter, Mr. Durman called upon the Vicar on the Saturday morning and informed him that he thought if the Vicar's suggestion was carried out it would give rise to another scene; but if the Vicar did not wish any singing in church he (Mr. Darman) would keep away on the following Sun- day in accordance with his request, and on condition that Mr. Pemberton did not play the organ. The Vicar stated that if Mr. Darman did not wish Mr. Pemberton to play, the latter gentleman should not do so, and thereupon Mr. Darman said he would absent himself from church on the Sunday. This, the vicar mentioned, was the suggestion of the Rev. Canon Whitley, but upon that gentleman being seen by Mr. Darman, he remarked that he did not make the suggestion, but the Rev. T. R. Matthews had been in conversation with him, and suggested there should be a pause in the services. While Mr. Durman and Canon Whitley were in conversa- tion, the Rev. T. H. Matthews came to see Canon Whitley, and the situation was briefly discussed. The Vicar ulti- mately said he was quite willing that Mr. Durman should play the organ, but he was not going to recognise the choir for their past conduct, because they had refused to sing on one or two occasions when he had given them an opportu- nity of doing so. He added that the choir would not be allowed to enter the chancel. but they must occupy seats in the body of the church. He instructed Mr. Durman to intimate that fact to the members of the choir, and Mr. Darman promised to do so. Mr. Durman asked the vicar if he was to be punished by being prevented playing the organ because the choir were ; bjectionable to the- vicar, and the latter replied that he was content with Mr. Durman's play- ing if the choir would not occupy their usual places. In the afternoon of the same day Mr. Durman informed the choir that according to the vicar's instructions they were to occupy seats in the body of the church, and not in the chancel, as formerly. This action on the part of the vicar so soon after theapparently friendly agreement created considerable excitement in Earlestown, and the matter was again brought before Canon Hopwood, who expressed his regret and sorrow at the re-opening of the dispute. Mr. Corlett, the late people's sidesman, afterwards consulted the vicar on the subject, but so definite arrangements were come to. We are informed that Canon Hopwood stated he was under the impression that the old organist and choir were to take their accustomed places; but the Vicar informed Mr. Corlett that when he accepted outside pressure he generally found himself in the wrong. At the service on Sunday forenoon the church was filled—many persons having evidently attended in the hope of witnessing another " scene "—for such was generally expected. The choir occupied their usual seats in the chancel, and Mr. Darman presided at the organ. The individual named Butterworth, from Middleton, who labours under the idea that he is Jesus" and " (Arises Ambassador," was again present, and made him- self conspicuous by moving about the organ, entering the vestry with the Vicar, Sec. He expressed the opinion that he would like to do something towards bringing peace in the parish, and offered either to preach, read the lessons, or ' blow the organ. Ultimately he was relegated to the post of organ blowing—a teak which he also performed in the evening. Before the service in the forenoon commenced the Vicar, speaking from the reading desk, said: Before I com- mence the service this morning, I wiah to say a few words. Doubtlessly most of you present have heard that something like a settlement has been come to with regard to the differ- ence which has existed amongst us for some time past. That settlement has been come to on certain conditions, and also by the arbitration of the Rev. Canon Hopwood, rector of Winwick-. I find that a great deal of misapprehension and misrepresentation is already abroad on the subject. lam not going to enter into the merits or demerits of this rain- representation; all I shall say is that on certain conditions the difference is settled. Some other few preliminaries have to 6e attended to before the thing is final. But I have no doubt that will be done, if not to-day, to-morrow. As there is a tnisipprehension in the parish, and repecially 1 from the report in the newspapers, which are always, or nearly always, misleading, I may just read a 'ewer I have received from Canon Hopwood, which is the basis of the settlement of our difference. "The vicar of the parish is supreme, subject of course to the bishop, over the service in the church, over the choir including their *admittance into and their discharge from it, over what is played in the church, and what is sung, and over the organ itself. Rules for the choir to be drawn up by the vicar. In case it is necessary to remove the organist from his office the vicar under circumstances where the organist is elected by the vestry, paid by the parish through the churchwardens, should consult the wardens and act, if possible, with their concurrence and assistance. The organist when appointed ought to be appointed subject to one month's notice of dis- charge. On the above understanding and on these terms I Mr. Durman is to resume by consent of the vicar his place as organist; he having apologised for anything he has done to the vicar's dishonour or in defence of his proper authority in the church." I have also heard this morning from , another source, which I cannot doubt or disbelieve for one moment, that in consequence of the reasonable, I thiuk, re- 1 quest which I neide through Ma Durmen to the choir that a greater disturbance thatl ever has to take place to-day, but why, I don't know. Certainly I don't intend to make any such disturbance. Of course whoever does make it is responsible for it and the making of it. The service was then proceeded with without any interrup- tion, the prayers, &c, being heartily responded to by the choir and congregation. The vicar gave out three hymns, which were sung by the choir and congregation, Mr. Dar- man presiding at the organ, after which the viear also preached. After the sermon the curate began reading the usual offertory sentences, but no collection was made, the sidesmen and other persons leaving the church. There was agent a large attendance at the evening ser- vice, which passed off, with decorum, everyone appearing to take a hearty interest in it. Mr. Durman again played the organ, and the choir occupied their accustomed seats in the chancel. Hymns were given out and sung, and after a sermon from the Rev H. E. Smith (curate) the usual offer- tories were taken, the collectors being Messrs. Corlett, Birk- head, Nevitt, and Burchall. It has since been ascert fined that the reason why no col- lection was made at the morning service was because the offertory " plates" were not handed to the sidemen by the vicar, and it would also appear that the vicar, when read- ing what are nowknown as the "conditions of settlement," kept back an important sentence. The copy of the " agree- ment" receive'd by Mr. Corlett from Canon Idopwood, and which was assented to by the parties at the interview last week, contains the following closing sentence :—" The past is understood to boon both sides entirely condoned, and they are to start afresh." It will I'S noticed from our report of the vicar's remarks be did not read this sentence—which so far as the parishioners and church officers are concerned, is looked upon as the most important in the " agreement." From the following copy of a letter, which has been handed to us for publication, it will be observed that Canon Hop- wood was very anxious that the whole of the statement should be carefully given to the public so as to prevent any misapprehension or misleading statements in regard to it. The letter was received by Mr. Corlett on Sunday morn- ing Winwick, 10.11 May, 1884.—Dear Sir,—lf the paper I sent to you yesterday finds its way into the news- papers, I shall be obliged that it should appear as a whole and in my own words, for one person gets hold of one por- tion and another of another portion, and so no fair state- ments gets publicity. I sent it to you because I thought in explaining to inquirers what was agreed upon, it was well you should have a paper or agreement accurately set forth. I do not wish any ostentatious public ition of what I sug- gested, but now-a-days everything finds its way into the papers either correctly or incorrectly. God grand you all a happier Lord's Day to-morrow and a right judgment in all things; and may the spirit of peace and love take the place of what has been so painful. Always the friend and well-wisher of you all,—F. G. Horwoon."

THIS APPOINTMENT OF WARDENS : A STRANGE " MFDDLE." A most singular and peculiar difficulty has arisen in Con- nection with the office of warden for St. John's Church 4 It will be remembered that at the Easter vestry meeting, when• the proceedings were of a somewhat extraordinary char- acter' Mr. George Appleton was unanimously appointed people's churchwarden; but the Vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) stoutly refused to name his own new warden, although he was strongly requested so to do by the parish- ioners. After a stormy scene the meeting elected Mr. M. Birkhead (late sidesman) as the vicar's warden. The annual q visitation" ef Chancellor Espin, for the purpose of what is called "swearing-in" the wardens was afterwards held at Wgrington, but on the application of the vicar the "ceremony," so far as the St. John's Church officers was concerned, was adjourned until May 13th. Accordingly ChancellorsEspin eat in the vestry of St. Nicholas' Church, Liverpool, on Tuesday, and the Earlestown case again came up. There were present the Vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews), Mr. George Appleton, Mr. Birkhead, Mr. Nevitt. Mr. Corlett, and Mr. Atty, the latter as the intended vicar's warden. div.head: PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH,
div.p: THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH,

The paragraph headed "St. John's Church and the Presbyterian Synod," in your last week's issue, deserves to be carefully pondered by those who desire to note the posi- tion and prospects of Presbyterianism at the present day. In seeking permission from the Synod to dispose of the present building i... Winwick-street, the Rev. James Warnock was understood to explain that "the church was not situated in a part of Warrington calculated to advance the interests of Presbyterianism, the majority of the people living in the neighbourhood belonging to the non-church- going class." They proposed to erect a new church in another part of the town ; "the change would not alter their position with reference to the town, except that they would be in a better neighbourhood. They were by no means removing away from the poor of the neighbourhood, but if anew church were built their position would be im- proved as regarded the poor of the district." "Removing to new and more commodious premises" is a step shop- keepers frequently find it profitable to take, the ostensible reason usually being the enormous increase in their busi- ness. The case seems to be different, however, with our friends the Presbyterians in Warrington. Their reasons and arguments supporting their plea for a change of quar- ters may be difficult to reconcile or understand. At any rate, they excite in the mind grave doubts as to the power and adaptability of the Presbyterian system to live and flourish amongst those who most need to be brought under the influence of the Gospel. Its adherents seem to sigh for a purer air and more aristocratic surroundings. Are they thereby better fulfilling their mission in the world? It is customary for church-goers of all denominations to. loudly deplore the utter lack of interest manifested by the masses in matters spiritual. But it is scarcely in accordance with the spirit of true Christianity to abandon them to their fate. Stiff and starched Presbyterianism will require a stronger recommendation than mere respectability before it can ever hope to discharge the whole duties of a church. To speak plainly, this same awful respectability has shrunk and shrivelled many a Presbyterian congregation to their present slender dimensions. Scotch ministers in English towns not nnfrequently mourn the fact that their countrymen in large numbers fall away from the church of their earlier days when they settle in the south. They might profitably supplement this complaint with the inquiry whether if Barns were to appear here and now, he could not find good reason to say what he said long ago—
As cauld a day as ever blew. A caulder kirk and in 't but few, As Vatlid s, minister ie e'er spak', s' be he or I gang back.

So rife is the spirit of exclusiveness, and so glaring the arrogance of superiority, the poor and the needy are repelled rather than attracted. Aggressive work all but neglected, or only fitfully undertaken; a large field reach- ing to the very steps of existing churches, and so far as they are concerned left uncultivated; the existence of the Salvation Army, with all its extravagant proceedings, be- comes not only possible but desirable. Whether the old building in Winwick-street falls into the bands of the Church of England, hr of General Booth, the revealed state of the neighbourhood should make every one of your readers wish them God speed.—Yours truly, Warrington, May 13th, 1884.
A. C.

PUBLIC CONTENTION.—A public convention was held in Trinity Chapel, Frodsharn, on Wednesday evening, when the Rev. J. M. Bamford presided, and there was a large congregation. The theme for discussion was "Christian life and work in relation to the enlargement of the Church of Christ," the speakers being Revs. Thomas B. Goodwin, J. Feather, Charles E. Beecroft, and Joseph T. L. Maggs. A collection was made at the close of the meeting in aid of the district expenses. • •

Cittrami MISSIONARY SOClETY.—Sermons on behalf of the above society were preached in the Parish Church, Frod- sham' on Sunday morning and evening by the Rev. R. Pal- mer, MA., late missionary in China; and the annual meet- ing was held in the Town Hall, on Monday evening, when the Deli.. H. B. Blogg presided, and addresses were delivered by the Chairman and the Revs. H. Palmer, M.A., and J. H. Acheson, M.A. A collection was made after each service and at the meeting in aid of the funds of the society.

BAINTIILLe st ittPonst tinin since we announced efiat the committee of this club were waiting for the due ' substantiation of right of ownership before completing the purchase of the Property to be used as a Clubhouse. The owners having brought the necessary proofs, the committee at once closed the bargain, and are, therefore, now possessors of a very eligible piece of property. Tenders have been issued for the necessary alterations, and it is trusted that in , a very short time the members will be in their new pre- mises.

FLORAL AND HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY. The annual meeting of the officers and committee of this society was held in the Boys' Schoolroom, on Thursday evening, the ilth instant, Mr. G. W. Rawlins in the chair. There was a good attendance. The treasurer announced that the ac- counts for 1883 could not be closed until all the outstand- ing subscriptions had been paid, and the sum of money tendered for the supply of refreshments at the last show had been received. Notwithstanding these rather adverse circumstances the committee determined to hold their seventh annual show in July. Mr. J. Rudge and Mr. W. Rawlins were re-elected secretary and treasurer respectively for the ensuing year. ATHLETIC FESTIVAL SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of this society was held in the Victoria Hotel, on Monday eveninz, Mr. H. Owen in the chair. The treasurer reported that the athletic festival of 1883 had been highly success- ful, leaving a good balance in his hand, and this had been further augmented by the proceeds of the recent sale of the [cricket pavilion, thus placing upwards of £4l to the credit of the society. Mr. Pickering announced that on behalf of the committee he had taken Mr. Warburton's field as yearly tenants at a rental of £l6 and rates. This places at the dis- posal of the committee an excellent field for future sports, or any outdoor games the society may feel called upon to support. The officers having been reelected, a vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the business.

that the parishioners bad power to appoint one for him. The Chancellor stated, however, that the vicar had a right to elect one warden, and the 'parishioners another warden, and therefore Mr. Matthews was justified in bringing his warden down. The Vicar stated that be would appoint Mr. Atty as his warden, and also said that he was not going to have any sidesmen in his church for the ensuing year. Chancellor Espin, however, replied that they would see about that, and, added be, to Mr. Matthews, "I never had my own way in my parish, and what is more, I never wanted it." The Rev. T. R. Matthews, however, strongly expressed his intention of not 1 having any sidesmen, and objected to Mr. Birkhead as the vicar's warden; whereupon Mr. George Appleton asked for hie name to be crossed out as the parishioner's warden, de- claricg that he was not going to serve unless he was sup- ported by proper church officers. He thereupon left the room, refusing to sign the usual paper presented to a newly. appointed warden. Mr. Appleton's refireinent created a difficulty, but this was considerably increased when Mr. Atty (who has been a warm friend of the vicar) expressed his intention of not accepting the office of vicar's warden unless Mr. Appleton was the parishioners' warden ; and be too, refused to Bien the warden's paper. After a little further discussion the gentlemen present, with the excep- tibn of the Rev. T. R. Matthews and Chancellor Benin, left the vestry and returned to Earlestown by train. The news of the refusal of the wardens to accept office spread rapidly throughout the town, and it was stated that the old wardens had signed notices resigning their offices on Monday night, thus creating a most extraordinary state of affairs. There are now legally no wardens or sideemen in the parish; and a mingled feeling of curiosity and wonder is being mani- fested as to what the upshot of the strange state of things will be, and what new phases of the squabble may yet be developed.

AN EARLESTOWN FARMER AND HIS DEBTS. SERIOUS CHARGES. At Warrington County Court, on Monday, the hearing of thi adjourned case of Hepworth and Co. v. Thomas Mort was resumed before Mr. W. Wynne Mulkes, judge.—ln this case a claim was madefor 38s by the plaintiffs Messrs. Heyworth and Co., debt collectors, 42, South John-street, Liverpool, against the defendant, Thomas Mort, farmer, Heal House Farm, Earleatown, being a twelve month's sub- scription in return for which tbe plaintiffs undertook to col- lect certain debts.—Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, Warrington, ap- peared on behalf of the defendant.—Thomas Moore, an agent of the plaintiffs, produced certain papers which he alleged had been signed by the defendant, or on his behalf, at his house on the 25th November, 1881, by which he acknowledged himself a member of the debt collecting society, and undertook to pay subscriptions.—ln answer to Mr. Jenkins, Mr, Moore said that on the day' in question he met the defendant near the race-course at .Newton•le-Willows and then accompanied him to a public-house where he had a glass of beer, and he believed defendant had a glass of spirits. They then went to defendant's house and went into the kitchen. He believed defendant's wife and daughter were also in the kitchen at the time, and if any papers were signed they must have seen it.—Defindant was then called into the box, and in answer to questions said he could write his own name but he did not make oat his own bills. His daughter made out his bills, and up to 18 months ago his step son used to make some out, At the time these transac- tions took place, however, his stepson was never in the house. On a piece of blue paper being handed to him de- fendant said it had never been signed by him or on his be- half.—Mr. Jenkins, in addressing His Honour for the defence, said it was admitted that the plaintiffs' agent went to the defendant's house on the day named, and that a con- versation took place with regard to defendant employing Messrs. Hepworth and Co. to collect certain debts. The plaintiffs' agent impressed upon Mr. Mort the necessity of getting in some debts which were owing to him amounting to £3l 148 sd. Defendant was quite as anxious as the other that this should be done, and after considerable haggling he agreed to become a member of the society in question for 12 Months. Defendant asked, if he could give the job up and the defendants' agent replied "Decidedly you can," and ac- cordingly to the defendants' version not a word was said about giving two months i notice before giving up. Nor did defendant sign any paper, and he (Mr. Jenkins) was in- structed to say that the plaintiffs' story with regard to the signing of that paper was &deliberate falsehood,and that the paper was a forgery. His Honour: That is a serious charge; you had better be careful.—Mr. Jenkins said he was instructed that it was a deliberate for- gery, and he was glad that the case had been adjourned' in order that he might prove the facts that he was now alleg- ing.—Mr. Mort, the defendant, • was then called, and stated that on the 25th November, 1881, be walked home with the last witness as stated, but they never went near a public. house. On reaching the house he paid his companion 30e, the subscription for one year's membership in the society in question, for which he received a receipt. It was agreed that if he continued longer in the society it was to be £1 is per year afterwards. He never, however, signed any paper as was alleged, and pen and ink was never used except by the agent to sign the receipt. The plaintiff subsequently sent him demand notes for another year's subscription, but he returaed them at once by post. —Mary Ann Mort, the daughter of the defendant, next gave evidence. She said she was in the house at the time of the alleged transaction between her father and the plaintiff's agent. She remem- bered the latter telling her father that he could give up his connection with the society at the yea* end, and she was certain that no one used pen and-‘ink •but- the agent when signing the receipt which he gave her father. On the piece of blue paper being handed to witness she said she could not say by whom her father's signature had been written uppn it. It was not her writing. • She then, at the request of the judge, wrote her father's name on a piece of paper and also the word Earlestown," and it was handed up to his Honour..—Ann Mort, the. wife of the defendant, gave corroborative evidencei after which his Huaour said Mr. Jenkins bad raised the !serious question of perjury and for- gery, and it was a question which he (his Honour)of course had to deal with. On looking at the signature "Thomas Mort" on the piece of blue paper, which was said. to have been forged, and on looking at the writing of the defendant's daughter he did not feel the slightest doubt in saying that she had written her father'i signature on the piece of blue paper. His Honour then described several points in the two signatures which he thought corresponded, and con- cluded by saying that the case might be a very fit one for inquiry•before the magistrates. The onlydifficulty he saw was that of getting evidence, because there were only three people present and there must be at least the evidence of one/person and corroborative evidence to show on which side the truth lay. He gave a verdict for the plaintiffs.

DLITH BY POISONING. On Thursday morning Mr. Brighouse, county coroner, heltl. an 'inquiry, at the White Hart Hotel, Sankey-street, Warrington, into the circumstances attending the death of William Thomas Breeden, 52 years of age, an agent, who died at his lodgings at 13, Kendrick-street, on Wednesday morning, under the following circumstances, as given in- evidence.—Heuty Dewhurst Breedon, son of the deceased, who also resides at 13, Kendrick-street, said that the dee ceased had been in a depressed state of mind through pecu- niary difficultiee, and not being able to meet his liabilities. He had had a singing noise in his head which prevented him from sleeping at night, and which had troubled him a great deal. He had only been under medical treatment for deafness, but for the last twelve months or so he had been in the habit of taking bromide of potassium to induce sleep. Wilness believed that his father ascertained from a doctor that 30 grains would be a reasonable 'dose to take, and witness knew from his own knowledge that be had many times taken that quantity. The paper produced was given ' to witness by his father, and he purchased the quantity of bromide of potassium stated ; he was sure that his father took the whole quantity.—At this point a reference was made to the sale of drugs, and the Coroner remarked that he held an inquest a short time ago where a person took what would have seemed to him (the Coroner), an enorm- ous quaratity of laudanum, but which only had the effect of making him sleep. The sale of narcetics was quite common.—Witness, continuing, said that when he bought the bromide it was wrapped up the same as an ordinary powder, and was not marked poison. On Tuesday morning witness went once or twice to see his father, whe was asleep, and as he (deceased) had a gentleman to meet, he endea- voured to awake him, but was unable to do so. The assist- ance of Dr. Smith and Dr. Joseph was obtained, and the stomach pump applied to the deceased, who, however, died on Wednesday morning. He had the best inedical attention up to the time of his death. To witness's knowledge the deceased ma Monday night did not take bromide. The bottle produced was found in a black bag in the bedroom of the deceased.—The Coroner remarked that the bottle had evidently contained laudanum.—Witness deposed that the glass produced was also found in the room.—lnspector Berry remarked tliat it had evidently been recently used.— Witness said what it was found on the washstand where a glass was usually kept. About a fortnight ago the deceased was very low indeed, and he used Words to the effect that he did not know what his life was worth living for.—The Coro- ner : From what you have heard of him do you think it is a reasonable probability that he has taken a drug intend- ing to take his life 7—Witness : Decidedly not; I believe it Was with the intention of getting a good night's ' rest to meet this gentleman on business in the morning.—Eliza- beth Pickton, 13, Kendrick-street, also gave evidence, and stated that during the four weeks the deceased had lodged with her she bad never heard him' say anything that Would lead her to think that he was likely to take his life.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect " that the deceased died from the effects of having taken a dose of some drug to Induce sleep, and that the deceased met his death through misadventure."—The Coroner: I think that is a very proper verdict on the evidence.

Rather some. Some months after their marriage, Mr. and Mrs. Rather,, were invited to spend the evening with an old friend of the former's,and as his friend was a prosper- ous manufacturer, and quite the ton, Jones expressed a hope to his wife before going that she would not make a fool of herself—a polite request she promised to remember. When they reached their destination they found, as a matter of course, that the first item on the programme was tea, and I it was during the discussion of that interesting subject that Mrs. Jones distinguished herself after her usual fashion. Glancing along the table she saw much that was good to eat and pleasant to the eye; but Was especially attracted by a plate of what appeared to be toasted tea.cake, which ,hap- pened to be her particular " wanity f' but not being able to reach it she called to her husband across the table, quite loud enough for all to hear "Robert, reach that toasted. moufin here," and then followed a profound silence that could be heard hi the next room. When the happy pair , reached home that night, Mrs. Jones broke her husband's seven-and-sixpenny umbrella by ronning her head against it, and if she had not gone upstairs something else would have been broken, as it was the cat caught it for about ten minutes, and it was not a mouse. t• RING OUT, WILD BELLS." The town of Mudborongh, in addition to other municipal instittitions, owns a bellmap, the said bellman answering to the name of Trotters, how derived history saith not. • Trot- ters has jingled his bell througlalludborough for years with both pleasure and profit ; but the other, day - its melodious music brought him; neither, but much other wise, Trotters Is a widower, and dirty at that, but it would appear that during his official peregrinations he had 'taken captive the heart of a " widow-bewitched," or a wonlan living apart from her husband. But such is tlie depravity of human nature, and of bellmen in particular, that Trotters ere long transferred his affections to another, this time a bona fide widow,—and we begin to think old Sam Weller's descrip- tion of this class of women about hits the truth. Of 'course this change would not take place without raising the suspicions of his last love, and consequently Trotters found himself in hot water now and again, for he had not taken the poet's advice to "Be off with the old love before you are on with the new," for the fact is the old love would not "be off," and as we have intimated, there were several skirmishes anent the new flame,but the other day came the 1 denouement. Widow number one heard the diphanous sound 1 of a bell at the end of a street, and she listened for ,the fa- miliar footstep; but it came not, and then, with fired I jealousy, she rushed form the house, and taking a short cut 1 to the street where lived the rival widow, when just as the I house appeared in view, Trotters disappeared from view. I Now for revenge, deep and bitter. Going up to the door, the outraged womart opened it without a knock, and, what a sight! There was nothing to see, only a bell—but the bell; ,Trotters must have been in the next house. However, not to be baulked-, she took the bell, and standing in the middle of the street, she rung out a " wild bell to the sky," and soon she was earnestly discoursing on women's wrongs, her own specially, to an admiring crowd of fellow women. Trotters did not appear, either personally or by counsel, perhaps he I objected to the jury. Therefore we suppose judgment went Iby default. How, when, or where he recovered his bell we know not; but the next time he appeared in public, be had ' the ten commandments plainly written on his face, and a 1 general expression of depression. HE WOULDN'T PAY. Before the introduction of the present types of restaurant and coffee tavern, the old-fashioned cook's shop was the only place where the pow wayfarer could buy what was, by courtesy, called a dinner, this dinner being either broth. I potato pie, or roast beef and potatoes. The broth and pota- to pie were dishes of mystery, wonderfully and fearfully I made, the writer never dared to investigate, but several times, yet never twice at the same place, has he been driven by stern hunger to try the other; but wherever tried it always was the same piece of beef. It was always tough and tasteless, reminding one of the Australian sandwich— too thin boards with a slice of lealier between -and the , potatoes appeared to be made of patty, ornamented with a number of small black holes. The serving was on a par with the food' the table was al Nays dirty, and decorated with a chipped basin at one end containing salt, and at the other with a gill pot without handle which did duty as mustard pot It was into such an establishment in a coun- try town, that a stranger entered a few months since, and asked for "four of beef and potatoes." Ile was served with ouch a plate as we have attempted to describe; but hungry as he evidently was, the antediluvian beef was too much for him, and, pushing it away in disgust, he called for a basin of broth. This was brought and his plate taken away, and a few minutes after, while trying to persuade his stomach to take the broth, another man entered and, seating himself at the side of the first arrival, called for " Four o' beef and potatoes," and when he got it he looked at it for some time in silence, and then he muttered: "I wonder wod these poritas us made on ?" and then turning to the stranger he said, "Did yo ever see such beef i' yore life ?" The stranger looked at the plate and replied, "Yes, I have; I've paid for that plate once." "Oh, yo'n had it, un yo? Well, I've paid for it too, bud I's ha' noan on't," and, knocking the table with the mustard pot until the waiter came, he said— " Ta' this leather an' putty away, an' bring some porita pie." The pie was no sooner on the table than a third person entered in the shape of a navvy, and he too called for beef and pota- toes. RUNCORN AND WIDNES. WESLEYAN DISTRICT MEETINGS AT RUNCORN. The annual sessions of the Liverpool Wesleyan District were commenced on Monday morning in the Camden Schools, Runcorn. The President of the Conference (Rev. T. M‘Cullagh) WB3 in the chair, and WAS supported by the ex-President (Rev. Charles Garrett); Rev. EL W. Holland, and Rev. W. 11. Tindall. After preliminary devotional exercises, the Rey. W. Tindall was almost unanimously elected secretary of the meeting, and he requested that the Rev. John ifornabrook might be allowed to assist him. Dispensations of absence were granted to the following ministers, most of whom are aged supernumeraries :—Revs. J. A. B. Malvern, J. M. Budden, G. 1.. Allen, D. C. Ingram, W. H. Sargent, Edward Jones, John Hearnshaw, T. lieeley, B. John, J. Harrop, T. P. Clark, S. Simpson, F. Friend, J. Aldred, and W. W. Duke. It was reported that two ministers had died during the year, viz., the Revs. Thomas Hughes and T. H. Hearne. The former was well known for the part he took some years ago in opposing the Methodist class-meeting as a test of church membership. Mr. Hearne was a young man, who died under painfully distressing circumstances, whilst suffer- ing from smallpox. It was resolved to forward a vote of cmdolence to his parents. The Revs. J. S. Workman and G. L. Allen asked per- mission to become supernumeraries—the latter for one year. The following are the statistics of church membership in the various circuits :

Liverpool (Pitt-street) ...v 490 30 30 Waterloo Birkenhead Sean ,mbe Chester Tarporley 420 34 41 old Carnarvon l4 11 Llandudno Holyhead Wrexham 548 26 Oswestry Whitelurcn 412 25 2 Warrington Runc.)rn Frodsham 213 7 Widnes 534 64 3 St. Helens 920 16 South( ort ( If ornington-road) 697 28 98 Ditto (Trinity) Ormskirk Wigan ... 20,486 1,148 522 325 The net increase of members in the district on the year is 197. It was reported that the following districts report an in- crease. viz :—First London, 587 ; Second London, 514; Third London. 150; Bedford and Northampton, 301; Norwich and Lynn, 195; Oxford, 28; Portsmouth, 141; Exeter' 259; Bristol, 451; Swansea, 153; North Wales. 96; South Wales, 77; Birmingham, 240; Macclesfield, 365; Liverpooi, 197 ; Manchester, 265; Bolton, 218; Sheffield, 84; Nottingham, 356; Lincoln, 95; Whitby, 177; Newcastle-on-Tyne, 197; Edinburgh, 263. In the following districts, decreases were reported, viz :-- Devonport, 396; Bath, 180; Halifax and Bradford, 742; Hull, 329; York, 158. This shows a net increase on the districts hitherto reported of 3604. The returns of the military were received from various depots. There are 113 soldiers and 69 in the militia. There are 772 young people in ministers' classes, an increase of 368. and 1891 in junior society classes, an in- crease of 187. The report of the examination of ministers was read by the Rev. T. Wilde, and was deemed satisfactory. A conversation was introduced by the Rev. J. A. Beet on the important question of the introduction of members into the Church. It was felt that there should be greater care in this matter.

The sessions were resumed on Wednesday. A large number of laymen united with ministers in dis- cussing the financial affairs of the church. It was announced that Mr. Richard Stead, of Waterloo, had died during the year. He was the treasurer of the Dis- trict Sustentation Fund, and also of the district branch of the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society. On the motion of Mr. E. Cannington (Waterloo). seconded by the Rev. T. Akroyd, the meeting resolved to place on record its sense of high appreciation of Mr. Stead's character and its deep loss in his death. .

The following seven ministers were elected to represent the district at the annual examination of ministerial candidates at Didsbury. viz. :—Revs. J. A. Beet, 54 votes; W. F. Slater, M.A., 48; H. W. Holland, 45; T. Wilde, 43; T. Akroyd, 37; G. FlPtcher, 34; W. H. Tindall, 33. It NM announced that the yearly collection in the classes amounted to £507 8s fld—a decrease of £6 Os id; while from the sama source £OOl 7s 2.1 had been received for the Worn-out Ministers' Fund, which is a surplus of £94 25 8d above the quota required. Special grants were made from the Home Mission Fund to the following circuits :—Carnar- von, £5O; Holyhetd, £5O; Oswestrv, £45; Welshpool, £35. The following circuits were reported as under obligations to provide an additional miaister's house, but were not able to do so, namely, Pitt-street (Liverpool), Mold, and Carnarvon. Reports of the Pitt-street mission and the District HOMO Mission Sub-committee were read be the Rev. C. Garrett and Mr. I. Mack. . .

The Rev. T. Carmichael brought forward the subject of Methodism at Hoylake and West Kirby, and reported the desire of certain Wesleyans in that neighbourhood to have a minister. After considerable conversation it was resolved that the matter be referred to the General Herne Mission Committee in order that, if possible, some arrangement may be made similar to that of the North Wales coast mission. Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst. Rhyl, was appointed district treasurer of the Sustentation Fund for a period of three years. The following eleven laymen were elected by ballot, after nom in ition, as representatives to the conference at Borslem —Messrs. T. Walton Stead, 48 votes; J. Mack, 45; H. R. Bowers, 44; G. S. Hazlehurst, 44; E Hutchinson, 42; C. Mitchell, 35; J. T. Warrington, 34; Henry Lloyd Jones, 29; Hincksmann, 28; E. Jump, 26. There were 25 nominations. The following elections took place:—To the Counexional Home Mission Committee, Mr. E Hutchinson; Extension of Methodism Committee, Rev. H. W. Holland and Mr. J. T. Warrington; Education Committee, Rev. T. Allen and Mr. E. Cannington. The Last conference adopted certain resolutions in refer- ence to the children's and schools' funds, to the effect that the mode of assessment should be changed from rates per 100 members to rates per minister, and that both funds shoald be amalgamated. These resolutions were sent down to the present May district meetings for their approval. The Liverpool meeting yesterday passed a relylution prac- tically adopting the proposed changes. Daring their stay in the town the ministers in attendance at the meeting have had the privilge of using the rooms of the Young Men's Christian Association, and Mr. Pownall, the secretary, has received a letter from the Rev. W. H. Tindall conveying the thanks of the meeting to the associa- tion.

div.head: TEMPERANCE MEETING.
div.p: TEMPERANCE MEETING.
ii

In connection with the annual meetings of Committee .of Wesleyan Chapels for the Liverpool district, a temperance meeting was held in St. Paul's Chapel, Runcorn. on Monday evening. A large audience assembled, and the Rev. Charles Garrett, the ex-president of the Wesleyan Conference, occu- pied the chair. On the platform were the Revs. H. W. Hol- land, J. Colwell, T. Rippen, Haigh, J. Anderson, J. Tucker, W. Barber, B. Lawn and G. Rack; Messrs. T. Nor- man and T. Simister._

The CHAIRMAN said he need not tell them that it was not a very heavy burden to him to consent to take any part in a temperance meeting. (Applause.) He had been so long associated with the temperance movement that he always felt at home when the subject had to be discussed, and they were met that night as Methodists to consider the question of temperance. Some of their friends might ask why this one vice had been selected when there were 30 many vices existing in the land. There were many answers that could be given to that, but one was that this vice stoott head and shoulders above the rest, and that it was not only gigantic of proportion, but withered and blighted and damaged every interest dear to them as Methodists, as Christians, and as patriots. (Applause ) Look at the fact that there were 180,000 places devoted to the sale of strong drink, and that those houses placed aide by side would make a street 750 miles long, and they would easily understand something of the enormity of the traffic. Look at it in smaller portions. In the neighbouring city of Liverpool he found that there were 3,000 houses devoted to the sale of intoxicating drink, and these houses placed side by side would make a street 24 miles long. Imagine 24 miles of drink shops placed in a city where they had a large number of population who had not been trained to self-control, and who were especially open to the dangers which accompanied this traffic. Wherever they vvent, whether in the magnificent city or the tiny haml.4. this evil met them, blighting everything they field dear; and he thought that they all felt that it was high time that the Church should do what lay in it power, in order to grapple with and destroy the evil for ever. (Ap• plave.) some of their friends said the temperance move- ment did not seem to have made much progress. He con- tended that the tereperance reformers had done a great deal. For instance, they had rectified public opinion. When he entered the ministry, public opinion outside and inside the Church WAS against them, but it was now on their side. (Applause.) Then they had changed the habits and cus- toms of society, and they had educated science: At the outset science was against them. It declared that drink was absolutely indispensable, but they had so altered that that now science was on their side. Dr. Richardson, the fore- most medical man of his time, said in all his experiments he bad failed to discover the slightest good done to the body by the use of alcohol, which is unnatural and always dangerous. (Appianso.) There might be a few doctors, voungdieciples living in the villages who did not take in the newepapers—(laughter)--who might not be of the same opinion. The temperance reformers had converted the chinch, and cow the Protestant churches and the Roman Catholic churches had united in holy rivalry as to which could do most to bring thic unutterable curse to an end. In

proof of this they had the temperance movement so incor- porated with Methodism that they could as soon eliminate the Sunday school or the Missionary Society from Methodism as they could eliminate the total abstinence movement. (Applause 1 They had also etruck terror into the trade. Fifty years ago the publicans had a proud position. Tne drink traffic was supreme. It was founded upon appetite, and buttressed by interest. It was defended by science and blessed by the church, and supported by everybody, but it had been struck a blow which mad made it tremble from one extremity to another. The speaker referred to the fact that there were fewer public-houses now than there were in 1860, although the population had greatly increased, and during the ten years from 1873 to 1883 the chink bill of the coun- try had decreased from 147 millions to 125 millions. (Ap- plause.) He concluded his address by urging those present to join the temperance movement. The Rev. H. W. HOLLAND delivered a humourous speech, concluding by expressing the opinion that there would be Parliamentary action on the drink question shortly, and he hoped that they would support those members of Parlia- ment who were determined that there should be some local control over public-houses—that they should have power to stop the erection of new ones, and power to revise old ones, and thus make the number much less than it is. The Rev. T. HIPPO'S, referring to the fact that he came from Warrington, said that place was notorious as a strong- hold for strong drink. It's breweries were notorious. Woo had not heard of " Greenall's pale ale " ? (Laughter.) The drunkenness of the Warrington people was notorious. At the last general election they were vary notorious because they sent a distinguished member of the " beerage " into political retirement and elected a man to vote straight for local option. (Applause.) They were notorious in Warrington, too, for their temperance principles. About two years ago they held a,gloi ions gospel temperance mission, and in two weeks took 10,000 pledges, and the converts of that mission were scattered over all the churches. Public opinion was in their favour in Warrington, and the press and the magis- trates had recognised their work, and altogether they were of good heart and hope. The speaker advocated the govern- ment of the drink traffic. .
Short gpeeches were also made by the Rsys. J. Colwell and J. Haigh, and the meeting c4ncluded by a collection on behalf of the expenses of the district meetings.

TEMPERANCE MEE I:ING AT WIDNES. A temperance meeting in connection with the annual meeting of Wesleyan ministers in the Liverpool district, was held at the Lacey-street (Weelevan) schoolroom, Wid- nes, on Monday, when the chair was occupied by the Rev. Mr. Kelsall, the other ministers present being the Rev. R. Harper, J. Hothersill, C. Bingant, and J. Haigh. The CHAIRMAN said that he was happy to be with them that evening, and he hoped that they would have a good meeting. Their object was to push forward the great cause of temperance, which, he was happy to tell theta, was malt- lag rapid strides all round the globe, and in America, where he had travelled, it had taken a deep hold of the minds of the people. The key. J. HAIGH (Liverpool), District Temperance Sec- retary, then addressed the meeting. He said that he believed that wine, beer, and spirit stimulation was bad for the body, and remarked that the medical profession was coming to the conclusion that it was dangerous and harmful. It sowed the seeds of disease in the physical constitution to which, without it, that constitution would be a perfect stranger, and it aggravated the germs of disease that already existed. Ile marvelled that men who were in the habit of guzzling so mach swill were not afraid of being swilled away by their guzzling. People asked for facts and he would give them. Dr. Andrew Clarke, physician in ordinary to the Queen, said that out of every ten cases of disease that came under his observation in the London Hospitals, seven were traceable either directly or indirectly to the use of liquors. Sir William Gull declared that liquor was a most destructive agent, and that large numbers of people were day by day poisoned by it. These were striking statements, and this professional testimony was borne out by the return of several life assurance societies. He opposed intemperance on physical grounds, and again, on the grounds of economy. The present was an age in which the subject of political economy was to the front. They had just been startled by the hater cry .of outcast London and the revelations of squalid Liverpool, and people were inquiring what could be done to stem the rising cry of pauperism in the land. He believed that the very best thing to be done was to erect against it the work of temper- ance. (Applause.) Nature was not niggardly in the dispo- sal of her gifts. She had given to 18,000,000 out of the 35,000,000 that constituted the population of Great Britain, it might be, enough he snpply their own wants and the wants of the remaining 17,000,000 of aged and young people and invalids, but she had given them enough to pro- vide for 216,000,000, six times the population of the United Kingdom, so that if, as they were told, there was a large army of paupers, there must be wanton and wilful waste somewhere. He believed that the main channel, the chief cause and opportunity of that waste, was intemperance. In twelve months the sum of £250,000,000 was spent directly or indirectly upon intoxicants, which would be sufficient to give to every poor family in the kingdom a bonus of £175. A c msiderable sum, perhaps one-third of the revenue of this country, was derived from this source, and the ques- tion arose was it wise to encourage intemperance on that account? To encourage the sale of intoxicants was simply to encourage the nation to drink its own blood. He also advocated temperance because he believed that stimulants were had for the soul, and that was the worst of all. Its physical and temporal consequences might be borne with, but when it pursued its victims into the invisible world and turned the key of the kingdom of heaven against them. it passed all possible limits and became simply intolerable. He (the Speaker) was a total abstainer himself, and he re- commended total abstinence to those by whom he was sur- rounded, because he believed first of all that intemperance was bad for the body, then it was bid for the circumstances, and then for the soul. It might be said that man had a natural craving for some stimulation, but it was just that craving that led to a great deal of drunkenness. Men often took intoxicants in the first instance for the exhilarating effects that they produced, effeets which were followed by dull stupidity. Drunkards were up like like a rocket and down like a stick. To over- come that craving he advocated religious influence and a close alliance between the Church and the temperance cause. He believed that the Church could do temperance work far more efficiently than any other agency for the simple reason that it substituted a legitimate method of stimula- tion. Let them as individual members of the Church awaken to a sense of their responsibilities in this respect. (Applause.) The Rev. C. BINGANT also addressed the meeting. He said that be believed in approaching the publicans with all possible kindness. Some of his teetotal brethren represented the publican as a monster, and he thought he hid heard it said sometimes that the public-house was a hell shop. Tak- ing the thing in a general light he should certainly not regard the publican as a monster, and he should hesitate in using the words "hell shop" in regard to public-houses. He could not see any great difference between the publicin who, according to his own idea, kept good order in his house and the man who drank his liquors. One sold the drink and the other drank it, and, he supposed, one was a publican and the other a gentleman.
During the pi:O-g-r-e;s of the meeting several songs were rendered, and a collection was made at the close.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. An ordinary monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday afternoon, in the Board-room, Alforde Chambers, Widnes. There were present—Dr. O'Keeffe (in the chair), Messrs. Carey, Holbrook Gaskell, jun., Houghton, Martley, Johnson, Sadler, Pankhurst, Forster, Wright, Midwood, Dutton, Webster, Allen (clerk), Capland (resident engineer), Higginson (surveyor), Carr (gas and water engineer), and Dickson (nuisance inspector).

, THE &HARMAN'S /lass/gm—The Clerk intimated that the first business would be to elect a chairman, as tile chair- man of the Board was now on his way to America.—lt was moved aria carried that Dr. O'Keeffe occupy the chair. THE PROPOSED NEW OFFICES.—The Clerk read a report by the surveyor upon the proposed new Board offices, and it was resolved that the further consideration of the matter should be left over to a special meeting of the Board to be held on Thursday. THE COPYHOLD BILL.—The Clerk said that letters had been received from Sir It. A. Cross, M.P., and Col. Black... burns, M.P., acknowledging the receipt of the letters from the Board asking them to support the " Copyhold Bill." THE LONDON WATER QUESTION.—The Clerk said the , next letter was from the London Water Compasies, suggest- ing reasons why the second reading of the Waterwerke Clauses (Amendment) Bill should be opposed, one of the reasons being that, especially in the provinces, the Bill would place the water companies at the mercy of the local authorities. It did not refer to that Board in the least.—The letter was laid on the table.

BOWER'S BROOL—lii;iier was read from the railway com- pany with reference to Bower's brook, and it being stated that i the chairman of the Board had this matter in hand t was agreed that it should be referred to him. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE.—The minutes of this committee contained as follows :—The Engineer instructed to obtain prices, ecc., of friel economiser. and report to next meeting.—Recommended that the Board advertise for ten- ders for a supply of gas, coal, and cannel, for periods of 1. 2, and 3 years, from let Jaly next.—Recommended that legal proceedings be taken against John Hill, of 3, West Bank-street, for damage to lamp.—The Engineer instructed to obtain some samples of gas cooking stoves.—Recom- mended that stoves for heating and cooking purposes be fixed free of charge.—Recommended that the Engineer at- tend the meeting on behalf of the Board.—Recommended' that the annual inspection of the Boards works be made next month, the day to be fixed by the Board. Water in stock, April 16, 8.449,878 gallons. The rainfall for the month has been :—Per gas yard stuage, -970 inches; per l'ex Hill guage, 1,035 inches; mean 1,027 inches.—ln answer to Mr. Dutton, it was stated that nothing had as yet been done with regard to the fuel economiser.—The minutes were then confirmed.—The Chairman stated that the proposed annual inspection was for the purpose of see- mg whether the property of the ratepayers was being kept in gc..ed order by the committees chiefly responsible for keeping it in good order as economically as possible. He thought it was a very important duly of the Board, and it wouid be a satisfaction to evert, ratepayer to have a good, honest, favourable report to show that the members of the Board were doing their duty to the ratepayers. It was for that purpose more than anything else that the annual in- spection was held. So far as the various committees were concerned—the Health Committee for instance—made a separate insPection of insanitary property of districts OCCi- ionally and iudependen, t of the Board, and the Highway Committee made an !avec:ion of at was under their

But the present inspection was the annual inspection.—lt 1 was agreed, on the motion of Mr. Ji.hnson, that the annual inspection shoald he held on the 25th June. tticinwev COMMITTEE.—The minutes of this committee I stated, with regard to the Waterloo-road Level-crossing, that a letter had been received from Mr. Shaw (London and

-- North-Western Railway Company) stating that he would give instructions to prevent unnecessary delay. The Sur- veyor handed in a report of the delays on certain days as In- structed. The Clerk was instructed to write to the Railway
Company again on the subject. The Clerk had also been instructe4 to write to the chief constable with regard to

damage to house property. Plan of alterations at Messrs. Walker and Co., West Bank Hotel, approved subject to the drains being constructed to the Surveyor's satisfaction. Plans of alterations by F. J. Simcock, John Hunt, and James Fletcher, in Albert-road, approved. ne Surveyor had re- ported to the committee that the footpath in Victoria-road between the London and North-Western Railway Co.'s bridge and Croft-street should be flagged, and the com- mittee recommended that it be flagged.—Mr. Johnson said he should like to know the reason for recommending the flagging Victoria-road. He thought the landlords ought to pay for the flagging as well as elsewhere.—Mr. Martley, re- ferring to Waterloo-road Level-crossing, said he saw the cor- respondence had been commenced once more. He wondered whether they might ever expect that nuisance to be done away with.—Mr. Midwood, in reply to Mr. Hartley, said the Highway Committee thought the Railway Comp toy were to blame for tbe continual nuisance at the crossing, and they had consequently given instructions that they should be again written to in the matter. With respect to Mr. Johnson's question as to Victoria-road. he said the subject was before the committee on the let of May, and they then considered that the parapet in that road was in a very bad condition indeed and quite a disgrace to that Board. The owners had been asked to bear a portion of the cost of flagging in the same way as was done in other parts of the town, and two replies had been received. One was from the John Shore, Leigh, estate, stating that they gave some land when the parapet was made, which they considered was a fair equivalent to the Board; and the 1 other answer was from Mr. Stringer, who said positively that ' he would not give one penny. Jervis' s and King. he thought, showed some willingness to pay something, but the com- mittee considered it would not be wise to take anything from one or two individuals. They would remember that some years ago the owners were willing to pay for flags. but the Highway Committee thought of trying an experi- ment in that street. That experiment was a complete fail- ure, and now the owners considered they could not fairly be called upon to pay anything at all. He thought that after they had once declined the offer of the owners they could not very well try to force—in fact they could not force—them to pay.—Mr. Johnson moved that this portion of the minutes be referred back.—Mr. Hartley seconded this amendment, which was, however, lost, and the minutes con- firmed.

THE RECENT LITIOATION.—After the minutes of the Sewerage Committee, in which there was nothing of public interest, had been confirmed, the Chairman said that the chairman of the Sewerage Committee wished to make a statement with regard to the late legal contention with Mr. Jeffries.—Mr. Carey then gave an explanation of the various incidents which led up to the recent action. He said they would remember that the contract was not origi- nally entered into with Mr. Jeffries but with Mr. Kirk, who, however, in March, 1882, relinquished the execution of the work owing to his private affairs, and they were all aware that tes filed his petition shortly afterwards. They were sorry that Mr. Kirk had to do this as he was a suitable man to carry out the work. Mr. Jeffries was after this *boson by the Board to carry on the work and he started in August, 1882 He proceeded with the work satisfactorily enough until September or October, but then a number of disputes arose between the Board and him. He had 15 months in which to do the work and the Board gave until the following Octsber. At the end of that time, however, Mr. Jeffries had not finished the work and they were then obliged to take it out of his hands as he proceeded with it so unsatisfactorily. They took advice on the subject, and it was largely owing to this advice, coupled with their own knowledge of the case, that they acted as they did. lie could say that during the time Mr. Jeffries was on the' work the committee did everything they could to assist him. Of course at the time the work was taken out of his hands there was a certain amount owing, the total amount being according to their tabulation £1,300. Mr. Jeffries thought himself very much aggrieved, and took an action against the Board, which was tried at the Manchester Assizes a few days ago, and he (Mr. Carey) thought they would all have read in the papers the tremendous speech made by the counsel for the plaintiff against the Widnes Local Board, makieg out their resident engineer everything he should not be, and the Local Board also everything it should not be. He had not got an account of that speech before him, but he remembered very well a great number of items it contained, and all those members of that Boaid who were at all ac- quainted with the case knew that they had a purely satis- factory reply to make to every one of the allegations that were brought against them. Well the case went on, and the first, and he supposed the principal witness for the plaintiff, was examined during the first afternoon and part of the fol- lowing morning. During that examination Mr. Jeffries' counsel made overtures to the Board's counsel for a settle- ment of the case, and the Board's counsel then communi- cated with the deputation on the subject. After discussing the matter they placed certain limits in the hands of their counsel. They considered that in all probability the case would be a very long one, and in the end would very likely be referred by the court to arbitra- tion, and they all knew how expensive arbitrations were; and they considered they should be putting the ratepayers to a very large expense, and although they had the very large sum of £1,300 in hand they knew that with legal ex- penses, &c., that sum would soon be spent. They thought that on the whole it would be better for them to accept something reasonable, than run the risk of the very large expense which would no doubt hive been incurred had they gone on with the litigation. The result of the agreement between the counsel on each side was that the Board should pay Mr. Jeffries £l,OOO in full payment of all claims. As he had just told them they considered that the Board owed Mr. Jeffreis about £1,300. They should probably have to spend £2OO on the reconstruction of a part of the sewer which was faulty, which reduced what they owed him to £l,lOO, so that after they paid the £l,OOO they would not be out of pocket. Each side had to pay its own costs. The result of this settlement they were advised by their counsel was a final one, and there would be no further claim of Mr. Jeffries against them. The thanks of the Board, Mr. Carey continued, were due to their solicitors, for they had carried on these proceedings, and he must not forget to mention Mr. Draper, who was Mr. Davies's assistant, and who had given very great attention to the business, and had made himself thoroughly master of it. He (Mr. Carey) also mentioned the services of the clerk, Mr. Allen, and Mr. Copland in complimentary terms. —Mr. Dutton asked if they were entirely free from any future claims from that t'• celebrated" individual.—The Chairman replier! in the affirmative—Mr. Dutton: I have been told that that is rather doubtful, and that there might be other claims.—Mr. Carey said the plant and material be- longing to Mr. Jeffries, and left upon the ground, would now be the Board's property. Mr. Jeffries could not claim anything for that, nor could he claim in any other way. 1 heir counsel and solicitors instructed them most emphati- cally and clearly that it was a final verdict, and that there could be no further claims made. HEALTH COMMITTEE.—In the minutes of this committee it was stated that the inspector reported for April that there had been three cases of typhoid fever, two of which proved tatal ; five cases of measles, three of which proved fatal; and one case of diarhcea, which proved fatal. During the month seven samples of milk were tested, and ranged from 213 to 31 by tha Lactometer ; and 328 oranges, 301bs. of fish, and 621bs. of onions had been destroyed. The clerk, Mr. Careyeadded, had been instructed to inquire of Major Cross upon what terms he would allow the wooden building to remain where it was. Before long he hoped they should have finished their plans and decided upon an infectious hospital, but until then they would want some temporary place togs to. LATEST NE Ws.
Yesterday the Queen paid another visit to the Duchess of Albany, at Claremont. _ . _

Lord Randolph Churchill was 'yesterday unanimously re- elected chairman of the National Union of Conservative Associations. No other candidate was proposed. At a Court Martial held at Dover yesterday, two privates in the York and Lancaster Regiment were each sentenced to two years' imprisonment for cowardice on the battlefield. . . . .

..- --...---. M. John Bright, who for some time past has been obliged to forego Parliamentary labours in consequence of 111-bealth, has arrived at Llandudno and taken up his old quarters on the Parade.
The Daily News understands the vacant see of Ripon has, by permission of Her Majesty, been offered to the Rev. W. Bsyd Carpenter, vicar of Christ Church, Lsncaster Gate, and Canon of Windsor.

A second Conservative candidate has at last been found to staad for Stockport. Mr. Nash's colleague at the next general election will be Mr. Tipping, who was returned for the same constituency in 1868.

SERIOUS EXPLOSION: FIVE MEN INJURED —An explosion occurred yesterday on the premises of the Bath Paper Mills Co., at Bathford, partly destroyed the works and injuring five men, two of whom are not expected to recover. A letter received at Paris from Cannes yesterday morn- ing says a report is current that Her Majesty the Queen is about to purchase the villa Nevada at Cannes to transform . .
into a:chapel in memory of the late Duke of Albany.

div.p: WAR RINGTON

PUDDLERS' WAGES—We have received somewhat late the following complaint from a correspondent signing himself "One Aggrieved," in reference to a leVer and foot-note which appeared in our last issue :—" In reading over the letter by Ex-Puddler,' I was surprised by the foot-note attached, which conveyed to my mind that the editor of The Examiner must be the private secretary to the gentle- man referred to, or that you had consulted the person in question as to whether you published the letter. Now, sir, I think the strictest secrecy should be kept by you, and if there is any defence to beoffered let it be made by the party referred to." Our correspondent is labouring under a singular misapprehension. There is a very simple explain- ' tioo of what he regards as a breach of faith. The letter in question appeared first in our St. Helens edition. It was printed and puldished en Friday morning, before "the gen- tleman referred to" knew that any letter had been written. On Friday evening we received the statement which fur- nished the basis of the foot-note, and saw no harm in let- ting it appear, in our Saturday's papers, along with " ex- Puddler's " letter. We certainly did not conceive that it could be open to such an anwarranted imputation as that made by " One Aggrieved." THE DISPUTE AT STOCKTON HEATH —The following is a copy of the memorial recently signed by over 500 of the inhabitants of Stockton Heath, in favour of Mr. licnson re- taining the post from which he is being dismissed :—" To the Vicar, Churchwardens, and Managers of St. Thomas's School, Stockton Heath.—We, the undersigned inhabitants of Stockton Heath and district, and members ot the choir and congregation of St. Thomas's Church, hereby express our complete satisfaction with the manner in which Mr. John 'R. Timson has fulfilled the duties of schoolmaster and organist of this parish during the past five and a half veers. Those of us who arc members of St. Thomas's choir desire to record our appreciation of the great ability of Mr. Tirnson as an organist, of his earnest and untiring efforts in training the choir, and of the great success which has attended those efforts. Those of-as who are parents of children taught at Stockton Heath school, have pleasure in stating that the seal with which Mr. Timson has conducted the education of our children has given us every reason to be well satisfied with his work. We therefore beg that you will kindly reconsider the subject of his dismissal, with a view to retaining his valuable services." We understand that the memorialists have as yet received no answer, but, as the matter rests mainly with the vicar, the Rev. T. S. Tofts, it is to be hoped that he will not set his personal feeling against the wishes of so large a majority of his parishioners. CONFIRMATION SERVICE.—On Wednesday afternoon a confirmation service was held in St. Paul's Church, Warring- ton, when the candidates were confirmed by Bishop Hel- muth, Suffragan Bishop of Liverpool. They were as fol- lows :—From St. Paul's and St. Barnabas Churches, 105 ; from Padeate, 22; from St. Ann's, 23;- and from Holy Trinity, 24. The following were amongst the clergymen present, viz. :—The Revs. S. Wilkinson (St. Paul's), E. C. E. Carleton and C. C. Harrison (Holy Trinity), W. H. Wil- liams (Padgate), M. Schonberg (St. Peters), and Richards ISt. Ann's.) In his address, the Bishop said that he need not dwell long upon that solemn rite, that solemn step that they were about to take. He took it for granted that it was fully understood by them, and that they were aware that they were declaring themselves in the presence of that large con- gregation and in the sight of God, to be Christians, not only in name but. in deed and truth, to be loyal soldiers and ser- vants of the Lord Jesus Christ. That, he said, was one of the most blessed days of all the days of their lives, if they were in earnest and sincere. He exhorted them to resist temptation by prayer, and to become loyal soldiers of the Saviour. What would they think of the soldier in the army who, whilst wearing the livery of the Queen was unfaithful, and was not ready to enter the field of battle, them bringing disgrace on the Queen's name ? Bet that was but a poor illustration of what was expected of them as servants of the Lord. They must be loyal soldiers of that great soldier who gave himself for them, and whose service they wets now entering. They must ask themselves if they could do less than give their lives to Him who had died, and suffered for them an ignominous and excruciating death. He urged them not to be merely professors but workers, asking what would be thought of a servant who simply professed and did not do the werk for which he was engaged by his master. He concluded by advising them to always keep in mind the text "Thy vows, oh God, are upon me." In the evening a special service was held in the church, where hymns appropriate to the occasion were sung. The sermon was preached by the Rev. W. Yates, vicar of Worlestone. The congregations at both services were large.

div.head: SALE OF WORK AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SALE OF WORK AT WARRINGTON.

On Thursday a sale of work, in aid of 5t...-inl;sMiti-sion Fund, was opened in the Infant School, Heath-side, by Mrs. Beamont, in the presence of a fashionable gathering of ladies and gentlemen. The walls of the school were very taste- fully ornamented with scriptural texts and suitable tnot- toes, and the various stalls were laden with a great variety of useful and ornamental articles, all of which had been ; contributed by those connected with St. Paul's and St. Bar- nabas', and friends. The stalls were presided over by the following ladies. viz. :—No. 1 stall, Mrs. Chorley, Miss Chorlev, Mrs. Murray, Miss Pendlebury, Miss Greening, and Miss Robinson • No. 2 stall, Misses Geddes, Miss Fraser, Mrs. Lowe, and Mrs. Proud ; No. 3 stall, Miss Lawless, Miss Ashurst, Miss Craik, and Miss Townsend. The St. Barnabas' stall was presided over by Miss Westwell, Miss Houghton, Ms. Highley, Miss Wood, Miss Braide, and Miss Minards; and the refreshment stall by Mrs. L. Greening and Miss E. Greening. At the opening of the sale of work there were present—Mr. and Mrs. Beamont, the Mayoress (Mrs. Harrison), the Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Robert Davies, Miss 'Wilkinson, Mrs. Tenn, Mrs. Greening, Miss White, Miss Robinson, Miss Lowe, Mrs. Proud, Miss Wilson, Mrs. G. Wood, Mrs. Wm. Burgess, Miss Comber, Mrs. Mewburn, Miss White, Mrs. T. Litton, and Mr. John Levien. The Rey. S. Wilkinson said that before their kind friend, Mrs. Beamont, opened the sale of work they would pardon him for saying a few words. During the last two years they had had a mission woman working in that parish who had been of the greatest pos- sible use to them in every way, but in order to have a mis- sion woman funds had ha6l. to be raised. They had found that the most effectual way of raising these funds was by having a sale of work once a year. He felt there was a special suitability in asking their friend Mrs. Beamont to come and open that sale of work in that-schoolroom, because they were standing epos ground which he might say was sacred to the Beamont family. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that Mr. and Mrs. Beamont for years past bad taken an interest in that parish, especially in everything connec- ted with its educational work. (Applause.) Therefore they felt exceedingly glad to welcome the presence of Mr. and Mrs. Beamont amongst them that afternoon. He believed the work they were engaged in was God's work, and that the services of their mission woman had been blessed. It was only the previous day at the confirmation they had in their parish that they had a number of aged and infirm women who were brought there by the special instrument- ality of their mission woman. The reverend gentleman concluded by saying that their warmest thanks were due to Mr. and Mrs. Beaumont for being present that afternoon. (Applause.)—Mrs. Beamont, in opening the dale of work, I said she had never made a speech in her life, but she did not think many words of hers were needed to explain the ex• cel lent work they were going to support that day, and for which so many of them had been working all the year, and she hoped many more kind friends would come with full purses to help them. She thought there was no such real women's work as that to be done when the wants and sorrows of their poorer neighbours and sisters were to be, relieved, when they were to be comforted and raised to something higher. Such she believed to be eminently women's work. She heartily thanked Miss Mackenzie for the faithful and very excellent way in which she had car- ried on her labours in that district, and which she was sure would be followed by a rich blessing. (Applause.) Mrs. Beamont then formally declared the sale of work open.
Mr. Justice Chitty on Thursday InAde an order to wind up the Oriental Bank Corporation compulsorily. There was no opposition.
