SMALLPDX IN LONDON.— In consequence of the con- t'nmid increase of small pox in London, the authorities, with approval of Local Govermnemt Board, have purchased at cost of £3OOO the river steamer Albert Victor, to act asp auxiliary to the hospital ships now stationed in the Lowe" Tnames.

DISTURBANCE IN IRELAND.-At Clonmel, yesterday, Peter Maguire was sentenced to ten months and other three risen, all privates in the Bth Regiment, to 30 weeks' hard labour each for riotous behaviour and window breaking. On Thurs- day the prisoners, whose conduct created dangerous excite- ment throughout the town, were arrested by citizens and handed over to the police. SPREADING OF SMALLPDX AT HULL A fearful out- break of smallpox has occurred at Hull. An Italian ice- cream seller, his wife, and family were attacked with the disease. The adults followed their ordinary calling, the woman goin from door to door selling ornaments and the children going to the Catholic school. The result is that more than.3o cases of smallpox are traceable to this family. Other cases are hourly being discovered. TRI CONGREGATIONAL UNION.- The Congregational Union met again yesterday morning in the Memorial Hall, Farringdon-street, London, this being the last day of its session. On the motion of Dr. Hannay a resolution was adopted in favour of petitiong Parliament on behalf of Sun- day Closing. An appeal was made for Lewisham School for sous of ministers, which has recently been transferred to a a new site.—The 11.6 v. Dr. Lees moved a resolution in favour cf the policy of Disestablishment, and a vote of confidence in Mr. Gladstone was also carried.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY SCOTCH TRAGEDY.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY SCOTCH TRAGEDY.

A lunatic named Hawe, who escaped from Dumfries Asylum, last week, died shortly after his re-capture by two keepers, and examination showed that the deceased had several ribs broken. The arrest of the keepers was ordered, but one had in the meantime committed suicide and the other escaped. RESCUE OF A SHIPWRECKED CREW.

The crew of the Liverpool steamer Illyrian, which went on rocks off Cape Clear yesterday morning numbered 68, all of whom esclped in the boats, and art at present quartered in Baltimore, Countl Cork, under care of Lloyds' agent. The vessel has rolled over on her side, and will un- doubtedly become a total wreck MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.

The Select Committee again met yesterday morning, when the examination of Mr. George Findlay, the general mana- ger of the London and North-Western Railway, was con- tinued. He said it was preposterous to suppose that if the canal were made salt would be sent to Manchester for transhipment whilst there was an almost free navigation direct to Liverpool. There was as mush likelihood of a wood market being established at Bradford as at Man- chester. Manchester could never compete with Liverpool for the export trade of Yorkshire, Staffordshire, and Derby- shire, though he admitted that canals and the sea had a great tendency to reduce railway rates. For the export trade the railway rates were lower than those charged for goods for consumption in the centres of industry. The town and dock dues at Liverpool were very high, and with the exception of London it was the dearest port in the kingdom. He did not mean to say that the Dock Board had not laid out their estate in a way which they thought the most con- venient, bat the connections between the docks and tin. rail- ways were not as satisfactory as they might be. STARVING A YOUTH TO DEATH.

A coroner's inquest was held at Croydon yesterday, on the body of Edwin James Sudbury, aged 19 years, who, it is alleged, was starved to death by Robert Bidgood, boot finisher, to whom he had been apprenticed from the Deaf and Dumb Asylum. The evidence showed that deceased, by motions, frequently informed neighbours that he was hungry, and when given food eat it ravenously. Recently he was observed to be getting very weak, and the neighbours communicated with Dr. Shuthouge, who examined the lad, and found him in a dying condition. A magistrate was consulted, but the lad died before his depositions could be taken. A post *torten& examination clearly showed that death was due to want of food. The body was dreadfully tciated, and only weighed fifty-five pounds. just half of what it should have done. Mrs. Bidgood, who was called as a witness, emphatically declared that deceased had abun- dant food offered him, but would not eat it. Ultimately the jury found a verdict of manslaughter against Mr. and Mrs. Bidgood, and they were at once taken into custody, brought before a magistrate, and committed for trial. The result of the inquest was hailed with loud cheers by crowds of persons who had waited outside the building. FEARFUL TRAGEDY IN LONDON.—TWO CHILDREN MURDERED. . . .

About seven o'clock ye-sterial;;;;;ln-g-, a man named William Albert Norris, who was liberated only a few days since after six months' imprisonment far house breaking, gave himself up to the police at Southwark, London, stating that; acting under impulse, he had stunned his two infant children with a rolling pin, and then almost cut off their heads with a large table knife. The police immediately proceeded to the house, and found the children—a girl aged three years, and a boy aged fifteen menths—lying upon the bed in their night clothes, with their heads nearly severed from their bodies. The children were removed in shells to the neighbouring mortuary amid much excitement on the part of a large crowd which had gathered. The prisoner does not seem to have been on bad terms with his wife who worked to support the family, and yesterday morning upon her leaving to go to her work in the city he kissed her as usual.

At Southwark police court, yesterday afternoon, Norris, who is a labourer, was charged with murdering his two children. Police-sergeant Biggs deposed that prisoner, who was quite sober, came to him that morning and told him he had murdered his two children at Kinross-street, Bermondsey. He said that he first stunned them and then placed their heads on his knee and cut their throats. Wit- ness went to the house and found the bodies as described. Dr. Gittens gave evidence as to CAUSE) of death, adding that prisoner told him that he could not see his children want. Prisoner was remanded, the inagistrates ordering that he should be medically examined as to the state of his mind.

div.head: FINANCIAL CRISIS IN NEW YORK.
div.p: THE FINANCIAL CRISIS IN NEW YORK.

NEW YORE, FRlDAY.—Messrs. Fisk and Hatch, whose failure was announced yesterday, state that their suspension is due to the long continued decline in the market pric.s of securities, the general weakening of confidence in financial matters, and to the heavy drainage of depoits. Mr. (latch has resigned the presidency of the Stock Efchange. A semi. panic prevailed in the oil market yesterday, arising from the difficalties on the Stock Exchange, and also from the failure of a bank in the oil district.

The House met at four o'clock. MISCELLAIPEOI7B.—EarI Cia.aNTILLy, replying to Earl Fife, said the information he possessed respecting the re- ported treaty between France and International African Association was cenfidential.—The Bishop of CARLISLE drew attention to the imperfect information issued with re- gard to great storms issued from the Meteorological Office. —After discussion, his motion for returns was postponed.— Earl GRANVILLE, replying to the Marquis of Salisbury, said refugees from Korosko and Berber arrived at Cairo and reported that General Gordon had made successful sorties, and was well.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The House met at the usual hour. NOTICE, &c.—Mr. Tommwsow gave notice that he would on an early day call attention to commercial convention between Spain and the United States with regard to the West India trade, and to move that in view of the increased difficulties in the British Empire by means of differential duties and bounty, it was incumbent on Her Majesty's Government to obtain the most favoured nation treatment. —Lord FITZMAURICE, replying to Dr. Cameron, said Her Majesty's Government were preAred to co-operate with the French Government in discouraping slavery in Mor- occo.

div.head: FRANCHISE BILL.
div.p: THE FRANCHISE BILL.

The House, in committee on the Representation of the People Bill, resumed the discussion on an amendment moved by Mr. S. Leighton to omit word and in first line of clause 2.—Mr. Gonszsepoorted the amendment. It did not strike at the principle of the Bill, but itA object was to make borpuqb and county franchise, in fact. identical.—Mr. ARNOLD opposed, and Mr. GLADSTONE said that the amend- ment would certainly have a disfranchising effect, there- fore be opposed it as he should all attempts to alter the basis of the franchise proposed in the bill.—Mr. J Low- THAR said he was opposed to every line of the bill ; there- fore he supported the amendment —Mr. LABOI7CUEUE said he still recognised Sir Stafford Northcote as leader of the Oppositien, therefore he asked him if the statement was

true 1.14 at appeared in the Standard, and thought Conserva- tives had entered into a conspiracy to defeat the will of the nation by throwing out the bill in the Lords. If it was to be done be thought it useless to waste further time in dis- cussing the measure.—After a long discussion, during which no answer was given to Mr. Lebouchere's question, the amendment was negatived without a division.—Mr. BRODRICE moved an amendment to the clause, the effect of which was to exclude Ireland from the bill. Mr. TREFELYAN opposed, and contended it would be madness to accept the amendment' The proposal, if carried, would tend to the most disastrous results in Ireland, therefore he asked the Committee to reject it —Mr. C. LEWIS said the Secretary for Ireland told the House that it wonld be madness to leave Ireland out of the bill, but he (Mr. Lewis) contended that it was the opinion of a very large class in this country that it would be a perfect act of madness to include that country in this present bill. He at great length insisted that the proposal of the Government was unwise, taking the present condi- tion of Ireland into consideration, that it would alienate the loyal supporters of the union between England and Ireland, and that it would practically place the House of Commons at the dictation of eighty ar ninety Irish mem- bers.—Dr. LYONS opposed the amendment and insisted that juetice should be done to a nation irrespective of individuals. PLIINEET insisted that the householder in Ireland was a very different person to the householder in England, and if the provisions of the bill became law the better educated and more civilised population in Ireland would be practically disfranchised by the admission wholesale of one particular class to the franchise in that country.— Mr. GLADSTONE justified the extension of the franchise to Ireland, and said no ground existed for the gloomy fore- boding after the passing of the bill.—Sir STAFFORD NORTH- COTE supported the amendmeat, as he thought the bill im- perfect and incomplete.—Colonel TOTTENHAM moved to report progress, and Mr. LOWTHER was speaking when the debate ceased in accordance with the Standing Orders. NEWS FROM Gortooer.—Lord FITZMAVRICE, replying to Sir W. Lawson, said that a telegram had been received that afternoon stating that refugeesibal arrived at Assouam from Berber and Korosko. They reported the roads open and quiet; thought Gordon had made several successful sorties, and was well.—The sitting was then suspended. The House resumed at nine.—Mr. LYNCH called atten- tion to the arrest of Michael Walters and others under the Irish Coercion Act, and moved that a Select Committee be appointed to inquire into the facts connected with the Crosmaglen prisoners ancl the subsequent release of Ber- nard Smith.—Mr. HEALY seconded the motion, and referred at length to the arrest of :Walters and others.—The mo- tion was negatived without a division.

G. Roberts, Major Cartwright, and Messrs. Derbyshire, Black- burst, Jolley, J. Humphreys, T. Hunt, R. Kilshall, N. Sid- deley, P. Worthington, G. Appleton, Caldwell, Brown, Forster, Grange, J. Greenall, and R. Owen, junior. TEE brmeTEs.—The CLERK reported that the number in the House was 268, as compared with 284 in the previous week.

SCMOOL COMMITTEE.—The Doctor reported the children to be in good health.—The Committee recommended that a suitable testimonial as to character and efficiency as school- master and mistress be given to Mr. and Mrs. Naylor, as requested by a letter from them, and that the resignation of Mr. and Mrs. Reynolds, of No. 1 Home, be accepted.—The application of the Rev. W. H. Williams, vicar of Padgate, for £lO per annum to be given for the use of the church on Sundays by about 60 children, was considered, and it was recommended that the application be complied with.—Mr. DARBY/HIRE proposed the adoption of the minutes. With regard to the pew rents at Padgate Church he might men- tion for the information of the Board that some 12 months ago an application was made by the vicar of Padgate to the School Committee, and it would be remembered that they I then gave a donation towards the enlarging of the chancel at Padgate Church—of £2o—and in consideration of that , the application at present under notice was deferred. The application had now come again before the committee and they considered that as they had already given £lO per an- num to the Roman Catholic Chapel at Woolston for pew rents, and as about half the children went there and the other half to Padgate Church, they should recommend that the application be acceded to. Mr. Darbyshire mentioned there was a book at the school for the use of the Guardians who might go at any time and inspect the schools. In the book any Guardian might make an entry or suggestion which would be considered at the next meeting of the com- mittee. There was also a book for the signatures of visitors. —Mr. CALDWELL seconded, and Mr. JOLLEY supported the resolution, which was carried. SCHOOL FEES COMMITTEE —This committee reported 38 cases in which they had allowed fees, and eight new cases, making a total of 46 fees allowed.—Tbe minutes were confirmed on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY. THE NEWTON SCHOOL FEES.—MT. APPLETON rose to remark respecting what was said about the Newton school fees the other week. He had been much surprised at the results that were made out by the officer's report. The report had surprised both the Guardians or Newton and the public, and consequently they had decided to overhaul the whole matter. Either they in Newton were doing a great deal too much in this respect, or at Warrington they were doing a great deal too little. ATTENDANCE AT THE Scwoots-=The SUPERINTENDENT reported that at the schools at Padgate there were attending 99 first-class, 69 second class, and 30 third class—total 198. Receiving industrial training 60 ;first-class, 48 second-class —total 108. Total of attendances 198, corresponding period of last year 165. THE AUDIT.—The CLERK reported that the auditor had attended the house, and so far as he (the Clerk) knew he had not made any repsrt to the Local Government Board against any of the officers. (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAN : That is very satisfactory. THE EXPENSIVE MEDICINE QUESTION.—The CLERK read a return of the expensive medicines purchased for the year ending Lady Day, 1884, as follows:—In No. 1 district, population 22,127, Dr. Joseph, and No. 2 district, population 28,626, Dr. Spinks, £lO 14s 10d; in Newton district, popu- lation 18,198, Dr. Watkins. and in Rizton district, popula- tion 1,271, Dr. Sephton, £26 19s; total, £37 168 10d.—The CLERK remarked that before he got the figures from the ledger he had really no kuowledge of the difference in the expenditure. He would suggest to the Board that the matter was one that should be submitted to the Relief Committee at Newton for report.--,Mr. DARBYSHIRE thought that it was the duty of every Guardian if he saw what he thought a flagrant and unjustifiable expenditure to call the attention of the Board to it. There was a matter that he should like to mention. The medical officers in certain cases were paid on a sliding scale. Was it a fact that all the cases that Dr. Watkins attended were those dangerous and expensive cases that were on the sliding scale. If not, he should like to know how the difference arose.—Mr. APPLETON was glad that Mr. Derbyshire had brought this matter of the medi- cines before the Board.—The CHAIRMAN said that if the matter were brought before the Relief Committee, they , might make a representation to the Board or to Dr. Watkins about it. He did not see that they could go into the matter • there.—Major CARTWRIGHT thought that Dr. Watkins should have an opportunity of explaining the matter.—The • CHAIRMAN said that he would do that before the Committee. , If he explained to the Committee and the Committee to the Board, they could than come to a conclusion as to whether or no the charges were reasonable.-. Mr. APPLEEON con- curred and thought that it was quite right that the Commit- tee should be charged with this duty by the Board.—The • Cmaistmate thought that such a representation would . strengthen the hands of the Committee.—Mr. BLACKIIIIRST then moved that such representation be made.—Dr. MACKIE thought that Dr. Watkins would prefer to report himself to that Board, rather than to a small committee of his friends and neighbours. He thought that they were all agreed that Dr. Watkins would be able to give a satisfactory explana- tion of the charges, both for medicines and confinement I cases. He did not know the nature of the diseases that prevailed in Newton, but if much quinine was required a • bill would soon run up. He thought that if allowed the opportunity the doctor would come to headquartors and ex- plain.—Mr. JOLLEY thought that that would be the best coarse to pursue.—Dr. MACEIE then proposed as an amend- ment, that it be left optional to Dr. Watkins to report either to the Newton Commissioners or to the Board. —Major CARTWRIGHT suggested that the discussion should not be reported in the Press, as in that case the public might at once come to the conclusion that Dr. Watkins had charged too much.—Dr. MACKIE thought that if the Major's ' suggestion were adopted it would be about the most unfor- tunate thing that could happen as far as Dr. Watkins was concerned. There had been nothing said that would at all ' compromise Dr. Watkins' character, as might happen if it went out, as it would be certain to do, that there was some- thing mysterious hanging over him.—After a little further discussion the original resolution and the amendment were withdrawn and it was decided that the clerk be empowered to correspond with Dr. Watkins on the subject and report to the Board —A discussion took place on a report of the working expenses, Jic., of the house and the schools, and it was decided that it be an instruction to the clerk to draw up uniform returns on the basis of the rateable value of the two establishments, and that the returns be printed. This was all the business of public interest.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that at a MEETING of the Local Authority of the norough of Wartiugton, held at the TOWN HALL. on WEDNESDAY, the 14th day of Mkr, 1884, the said Local Authority pursuant to an authority, of the Privy Coun- cil of the 10th May, 1884, and of every other power enabling them in this behalf for the purpose of preventing the spreading of Swine Fever, made the regulations following, that is to lay:- I.—These regulations shall commence and take effect from and immediately after the 17th day of May instant, and shall continue in force until the 30th day of June next, unless sooner revoked or altered by the Local Authority of the Borough of Warrington. 2.—No bwine shall he moved into the Borough of Warring- ton which shall within 14 days immediately prrceding suchl movement have beeu within the District of Widnes, in the county of Lancaster, or have been lauded from Ireland. The foregoing regulations shall not restrict the movement of Swine by Railway through the Borough of Warrington. WM. WY BROOK, Town Clerk.
